items.title: What Governance Actually Means
items.summary: Governance is the system of decision rights, accountability and assurance that turns stated intent into controlled outcomes. It is not the same as management, and it is not a synonym for compliance. This lesson separates the three, shows what a working governance arrangement produces, and explains where a GRC professional actually adds value inside it.
objectives: Define governance as a system of decision rights, accountability and assurance rather than a set of documents
Distinguish governance from management, from compliance and from oversight, using worked organisational examples
Explain what a functioning governance arrangement produces and what a broken one looks like
Position the GRC professional inside a governance arrangement and describe what good looks like

sections.heading: Governance is a system, not a document
sections.body:
The most common misunderstanding about governance comes from equating it with the artifacts that surround it - the board pack, the committee terms of reference, the policy library. Those artifacts exist because governance is happening, in the same way that a payslip exists because payroll is happening. Remove the payslip and payroll does not stop; remove the governance apparatus and decision-making does not stop either, it simply stops being directed, documented and challengeable. That is the actual risk.

Governance is the arrangement by which an organisation is directed and controlled. Three elements sit at its core: decision rights (who is allowed to decide what), accountability (who answers for the outcome of that decision), and assurance (who independently confirms that the arrangement is working). Remove any one of the three and you have something that looks like governance but is not. An organisation with clear decision rights but no accountability produces fast decisions nobody owns. An organisation with accountability but no assurance produces confident reporting that may or may not be true.

Think about it as a plumbing analogy, which is crude but useful. Management is the water: the operational flow of decisions, resources and work that actually gets things done. Governance is the pipework: the design, the boundaries, the valves and the inspection regime that determines whether the water goes where it should, at the pressure it can safely carry. Most of what a GRC professional does is not making decisions; it is making sure that the pipes are right, that the boundaries are known, and that somebody is checking.

A useful test: if the executive team disappeared tomorrow, would the organisation still be directed and controlled? If yes, you have management with good processes. If no - if the absence of particular individuals would cause the organisation to drift, stop being accountable, or start making decisions outside its mandate - then what was missing was governance.
bullets: Decision rights: who decides, under what delegation, with what escalation trigger
Accountability: a named owner for every material risk, decision and obligation
Assurance: an independent check that the arrangement is actually operating
Direction and control: setting intent, then verifying that the organisation is still pursuing it
sections.callout: Governance is what makes accountability possible. If no one can name who owns an outcome, no one can be accountable for it, and the word is just a label on a slide.

sections.heading: The questions governance must be able to answer
sections.body:
In any organisation - a bank, a hospital trust, a ministry, a factory - governance is doing its job if the following questions have defensible answers, and if those answers are current.

First: what are we trying to achieve, and how do we know? This is the objective question. It sounds trivial and it is where most governance failures start. When a strategy cannot be expressed as a small number of measurable objectives, every downstream risk decision becomes a negotiation. You cannot apply risk appetite to a strategy you cannot state.

Second: what could prevent us achieving it? This is the risk question, and it is where risk management attaches to governance rather than sitting beside it. Governance converts a risk assessment into a decision about resources, constraints or appetite - and it makes that decision at a level where trade-offs can actually be made.

Third: are we within the boundaries set by law, regulation, contract and our own policies? This is the compliance question. It is the part of governance that most easily becomes a compliance function in isolation, which is a mistake: a compliance issue that is not connected to an objective and a risk is a rule with no purpose.

Fourth: can we prove it? This is the assurance question, and it is the one most often skipped in the middle of the year, then reconstructed painfully under regulatory or audit pressure. Governance without contemporaneous evidence forces the organisation to argue from memory, and memory is not a control.

Fifth: who acts when it goes wrong? This is the escalation question, and it is where well-designed governance distinguishes itself from well-documented governance. A governance arrangement that describes what happens when everything is fine but has no defined path for the exceptional case is half-built. Every committee charter you inherit should be tested against that scenario before you trust it.
bullets: Objective: what are we trying to achieve and how will we know?
Risk: what could prevent us achieving it, and what are we doing about it?
Compliance: are we inside the boundaries set by obligation and policy?
Assurance: can we prove all of the above, contemporaneously?
Escalation: who acts, and how fast, when something goes wrong?

sections.heading: Governance is not the same as any of its neighbours
sections.body:
Four confusions cause most of the early-career difficulty in GRC, and naming them early is worth the time.

The first confusion is governance versus compliance. Compliance is one input to governance, not a synonym for it. An organisation can be fully compliant and still be badly governed - think of a company that meets every regulatory filing requirement while having no control over its own supply chain. Conversely, a well-governed organisation will usually be compliant, because it manages its obligations deliberately rather than reacting to them.

The second confusion is governance versus oversight. Oversight is the detective function - monitoring, auditing, investigating, challenging. Governance is the whole system, of which oversight is a part. The senior practitioner mistake is to build a beautiful oversight capability with no decision rights behind it: the audit committee receives a well-evidenced report about a risk nobody is authorised to fix. Oversight without decision rights produces a very expensive diary.

The third confusion is governance versus management, discussed above. Watch for the giveaway: if the person describing governance is describing what people do all day, they are describing management.

The fourth confusion is governance versus culture. Culture matters enormously, but governance is the formal, auditable part of the system - the part that works when the people running it are tired, under pressure, or new. Culture is what makes governance work when the formal machinery is absent. A strong culture with weak governance fails during a hostile period; weak culture with strong governance produces slow, grinding, well-evidenced failure.
sections.callout: A useful discipline for a GRC professional: whenever you hear a claim about governance in a meeting, ask which of the five questions it answers. If it answers none of them, it is probably an activity, not governance.
table: Do we behave as intended when unwatched?

sections.heading: What a governance arrangement produces
sections.body:
Governance is intangible; its outputs are concrete. A mature organisation's governance arrangement produces a recognisable set of artefacts, and you can use them as a diagnostic. If the artefacts are missing, weak or stale, the governance is weak - regardless of how many committees exist.

The core outputs are: a small number of board-approved objectives with named owners; a defined delegation of authority showing who can commit the organisation to what; a maintained set of policies that are current, approved and actually communicated; a risk appetite statement that is specific enough to be applied to a decision; a risk register that reflects the organisation's real exposures and is reviewed on a cycle; a schedule of committee meetings that actually happens with papers prepared in advance; minutes that record decisions rather than discussion; and a tracking mechanism that shows whether decisions taken in the room were actually implemented.

Two of those deserve particular attention because they separate a real governance arrangement from a decorative one. The first is the tracking of decisions. Governance that produces decisions but does not track implementation is a talk shop with a chart of accounts. The second is the currency of the artefacts. A policy set last reviewed in 2016 for a business that has since migrated to the cloud describes a company that no longer exists.

A useful way to test a governance arrangement is the delegation test. Take three decisions your organisation makes regularly - approving a capital expenditure of half a million, onboarding a vendor that will handle customer data, and taking a system offline during an incident. For each one, ask: who decides, on what basis, with what evidence in front of them, and to whom do they report the outcome? If any of those four answers is unclear, you have found a governance gap worth reporting.
bullets: Objectives with named owners, reviewed by the board at least annually
Delegation of authority that reflects how the organisation actually decides
Current, approved, communicated policies with a review cycle and a named owner
Risk appetite that can be applied to a specific decision without debate
Board and committee papers issued in advance, with minutes that record decisions
A tracked action list showing whether decisions were implemented
sections.callout: If a governance meeting ends without a decision, a named owner and a date, the meeting was not governance. It was a briefing.

sections.heading: Where a GRC professional fits
sections.body:
The GRC role is frequently misunderstood as a reporting function - someone who compiles a board pack and a heat map. That is the visible 20 per cent and it is the least valuable part of the job. The valuable part is designing and running the machinery that makes governance possible, and then being the person who can tell the board, without hedging, where the organisation's management attention is genuinely required.

Concretely, a competent GRC professional does four things. They establish the structures: the committee calendar, the reporting templates, the risk register taxonomy, the issue and escalation protocol. They make the connections: linking a control weakness to an objective, linking a regulatory obligation to a risk, linking a risk to a capital or headcount request. They test the machinery: running the reviews, chasing the actions, verifying that the numbers in the pack trace back to source. And they protect the integrity of the reporting - the discipline of saying what is not known as clearly as what is.

That last point is what makes a GRC professional credible with a board. Boards can tolerate bad news; they cannot tolerate discovering that the good news was wrong. A GRC function that smooths the picture for a quarter is destroyed the first time a real issue surfaces, and it will never be trusted again. Conversely, a GRC function that reliably tells the board the truth, including about its own failures, becomes the function the board leans on - and that is where a career is built.

The practical starting point for a newcomer: learn one domain deeply enough to be useful - risk, compliance, internal audit or security - and understand how it connects to the others. Depth without connections makes you a specialist; connections without depth make you a generalist nobody trusts. The enterprise GRC lead is usually someone who started with depth, learned the connections, and can hold an organisation's whole control architecture in mind.
bullets: Design: establish the structures, cycles, taxonomies and protocols
Connect: link controls to objectives, obligations to risks, risks to resourcing
Test: run the reviews, chase actions, trace reported numbers back to source
Protect integrity: report what is not known as clearly as what is

examples.title: A regional bank that had committees but no governance
examples.context: A mid-sized retail and commercial bank had a full calendar: board, risk committee, audit committee, credit committee. Board packs were substantial, minutes were long, and every meeting happened. But over two years the bank had twice approved acquisitions without a documented post-merger control review, and the internal audit function had reported the same three findings for four consecutive cycles with no management action recorded at board level. The chair asks you, as the new head of GRC, to explain why the bank's governance is ineffective when all the committees exist.
examples.outcome: The diagnosis is that the bank has management and reporting, not governance. Decision rights are undocumented, so approvals happen without a record of what was considered. There is no tracking of decisions, so actions never close. And assurance reports are received without a mandated response, so independent findings die on the table. The remedy is unglamorous: a delegation of authority, a tracked action register owned by the company secretary, a mandatory management response to every audit finding rated above a threshold, and a first post-acquisition control review. The chair leaves the session understanding that committees are a form, not the substance.

examples.title: Governance in a clinical setting
examples.context: A teaching hospital network has an information governance committee that meets quarterly to review privacy incidents. The committee has no written terms of reference, no escalation path to the trust board, and no decision about who may close an incident. A junior GRC officer notices that two serious data breaches in the past year were discussed at the committee but never escalated, because the committee believed that reporting to the board would create a regulatory referral. You are asked to redesign the governance arrangement.
examples.outcome: The redesign separates three things that had been conflated: the operational incident review, which stays with management; the aggregate and trend view, which goes to the risk committee; and the individual serious incident, which has a mandatory and time-boxed escalation route to the board and the regulator, with the legal and clinical duty-holder making the referral decision rather than the committee. Written terms of reference, a decision log, a defined severity model, and a closure standard (evidence of correction plus a control change, not an undertaking) produce an arrangement the board can rely on. The key insight delivered to the trust chair is that governance is about routing decisions to where the authority to decide actually sits.

practicalExercise.title: Map the governance of a company you know
practicalExercise.brief: Choose an organisation you have real or well-researched knowledge of - your employer, a family business, a university, a charity. Apply the five governance questions from this lesson and produce a one-page diagnostic that names what works, what is missing, and what you would change first. Write it as if it were going to the board, because the exercise is about board-level communication, not about listing concepts.
steps: Identify the organisation's stated objectives and where they are recorded. Note any objective you cannot find written down.

Take three recurring decisions - one financial, one operational, one involving an obligation - and for each write down who decides, on what basis, with what evidence, and to whom they report the outcome.

Check for the six governance outputs listed in the lesson: objectives with owners, delegation of authority, current policies, risk appetite, decision-tracking action list, and board/committee papers and minutes. Mark each present, partial or absent.
Identify the escalation path for an exceptional event (a serious breach, a failed audit, a regulatory concern) and note where the path is ambiguous.
Write the diagnostic: three strengths, five gaps ordered by consequence, and one recommended first change with the reasoning stated in two sentences.
practicalExercise.deliverable: A one-page governance diagnostic with a table of the five governance questions answered, the six-output checklist marked, and a prioritised gap list with one recommended first change.
evaluationCriteria: Every governance question is answered with a specific reference to how the organisation actually works, not a generic statement
Decision rights for the three sampled decisions are traced to a named role or forum, not described as management
Gaps are ordered by consequence to the organisation, with an explicit judgement about which gap matters most and why
The recommended first change is realistic for a single person to influence and is expressed in terms the board would use
The document reads as a board paper: no unexplained jargon, no lecture, no more than 500 words of narrative

references: ISO 31000:2018, Risk management - Guidelines, Clause 4 (Context and Guidelines) and Clause 5 (Framework and Process)
COSO Internal Control: Integrated Framework (2013), Principle 1 and Principle 3
Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission, Enterprise Risk Management: Integrating with Strategy and Performance (2017)
The Institute of Internal Auditors, Global Internal Audit Standards (effective January 2025), Domain 1: Governance
OECD Principles of Corporate Governance (2023 revision)
UK Corporate Governance Code (FRC), Provision C - Effective and Transparent Risk Management and Internal Control

items.title: What Risk Management Actually Means
items.summary: Risk management is the coordinated activity of driving risk to an acceptable level in support of objectives - not a scoring exercise and not a register. This lesson covers the risk cycle, uncertainty versus hazard, inherent and residual risk, the risk appetite chain, treatment options including acceptance and transfer, and the practical difference between a live risk process and a dead one.
objectives: Define risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives, distinguishing it from hazard and from issue
Explain inherent, residual and acceptable risk and the role of controls in each transition
Apply the four treatment options - modify, avoid, share, accept - with a clear justification for each
Diagnose whether a risk register is a live management instrument or a reporting artifact

sections.heading: Risk is uncertainty, and that changes everything
sections.body:
ISO 31000:2018 defines risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives. The keyword is uncertainty. A hazard is a known source of potential harm - a chemical spill, a credit default, a phishing email - where the event itself may or may not occur. A risk is the uncertainty about whether that event occurs and what it does if it does. When the outcome is already determined, it is not a risk; it is an issue, and it belongs on an action log, not a risk register.

This distinction has hard practical consequences. If a control has already failed and a breach has already occurred, no amount of additional risk treatment will help - the exposure is now a fact and the work is remediation, recovery and disclosure. Sceptics will also ask why we spend money managing a risk that has already happened; the honest answer is that we do not, and a risk register that contains realised events is telling you the organisation is running its register as an incident log.

The same logic applies to opportunities. Risk management in the modern sense covers uncertainty in both directions: a threat that prevents an objective and an opportunity that might advance one. Most organisations manage threats well and opportunities badly, which is why the strategy conversation is usually more interesting than the control conversation. ISO 31000 treats them symmetrically, and COSO's ERM framework explicitly folds opportunity into the performance dimension.

A third distinction worth making early: risk is not the same as impact, and it is not the same as vulnerability. Impact is the consequence if the event happens. Vulnerability is the condition that makes the event more likely or more severe. Risk is the combination. The reason this matters for a GRC professional is that every framework you will use - ISO 31000, COSO ERM, NIST SP 800-30, an internal audit risk assessment - expresses that combination differently, and you will be asked to translate between them.
bullets: Hazard: a known source of potential harm (a source of risk)
Risk: the uncertainty of an event occurring and the consequences if it does
Issue: an event that has already occurred - not a risk, an action item
Impact: the consequence if the event occurs
Vulnerability: the condition that makes an event more likely or more severe
Opportunity: uncertainty with a potential positive outcome - in scope, and usually neglected
sections.callout: If you cannot state the uncertainty and the objective in the same sentence, you do not have a risk statement yet. Try: the risk of [uncertainty event] affecting [objective], leading to [consequence].

sections.heading: Inherent, residual, acceptable
sections.body:
Three terms carry almost all of the practical weight in risk management, and they are used inconsistently in most organisations. Get them right and the rest of the discipline falls into place.

Inherent risk is the risk exposure in the absence of any controls. It describes the exposure the organisation would have if it did nothing at all. This is a hypothetical baseline used to judge whether a control is worth having; it is not the current exposure and should never appear in a board pack as if it were.

Residual risk is the exposure that remains after the controls you actually have are operating as intended. This is the real current exposure, and it is the number that should drive appetite decisions. The difficulty is that residual risk is only meaningful if you are confident the controls work. If control effectiveness is unverified, residual risk is an estimate resting on an assumption, and that assumption needs to be visible.

Acceptable risk (or tolerable risk, or risk accepted in accordance with appetite) is the level of exposure the organisation has decided it will live with given its objectives. This is the decision, not the measurement. The measurement is residual risk; the decision is whether that residual risk sits inside the appetite the board has set.

The chain that matters is: inherent risk, less the effect of controls, gives residual risk, compared against appetite, gives a decision to accept, treat further, or escalate. A GRC process that jumps from inherent risk straight to appetite comparisons is broken, because it assumes controls work without testing anything.

There is a useful discipline here that many mature organisations adopt: control effectiveness is only asserted where it has been independently tested. Everything else is an assumption, and assumptions are labelled as such. You will see this in ISO 27001 (where the Statement of Applicability and the risk treatment plan carry the assumptions), in NIST SP 800-53 (where control assessment results drive residual risk), and in COSO (where the internal control component becomes the bridge from inherent to residual).
table: What is the exposure with no controls?
Used as if it were the current exposure
What level of exposure is permitted?
Left as a slogan with no thresholds
sections.callout: Residual risk without a stated control effectiveness assumption is a guess with a decimal point. Always show the assumption with the number.

sections.heading: The risk cycle: identify, analyse, evaluate, treat, monitor
sections.body:
ISO 31000:2018 sets out a process with a recognisable shape, and almost every mature risk process on the planet maps onto it, whatever their labels.

Identification is the systematic sweep for risks - the deliberate hunt for things that could go wrong, as opposed to the accidental recording of things that already have. Identification should be driven by method: structured interviews and workshops, analysis of the risk register, review of external events and near misses, audits and assurance findings, and analysis of the organisation's own objectives and value chain. The output is a set of well-written risk causes (not events) tied to objectives.

Analysis is the quantification or qualitative characterisation of each risk: likelihood, impact, and sometimes velocity, controllability, and level of exposure. The discipline here is consistency. A risk register in which one team's likelihood means probably and another's means possible is worse than useless - it produces comparison errors that propagate all the way to the board.

Evaluation is the step that most often gets skipped and most often should not be. Evaluation asks whether the analysed risk is acceptable, whether it needs treatment beyond what exists, whether it needs to be shared or transferred, or whether the organisation should not be doing this activity at all. Without evaluation, analysis produces numbers that nobody has interpreted.

Treatment is the decision and implementation of options: modify (change the activity or add controls), avoid (stop the activity or change it so the risk cannot occur), share (transfer a portion, typically through insurance or contracts), or accept (consciously take it, usually with a named acceptor and often a time limit and monitoring). Treatment must produce a risk treatment plan with owners and dates, and it must be reviewed for new or changed risks rather than treated as a one-off.

Monitoring and review closes the loop. Risk profiles change as the organisation changes - new products, new systems, new acquisitions, new regulation. A risk process that produces a register once a year and then forgets it is not a cycle; it is an inventory.
bullets: Identify: systematic, method-driven, produces risk causes tied to objectives
Analyse: consistent likelihood and impact scales, with the scale documented
Evaluate: interprets the analysis against appetite and mandates a decision
Treat: modify, avoid, share or accept - each with owner, date and monitoring requirement
Monitor: track the treatment plan, watch for change, re-profile as the organisation changes

sections.heading: Risk appetite, tolerance and the decision to accept
sections.body:
Acceptance is the treatment option that most often goes wrong, because it is the one that requires no spending. Risk acceptance means the organisation consciously continues with the exposure, with someone senior enough and informed enough to make that call, and with a record of why.

An acceptance decision needs four things and usually gets only one. It needs a named acceptor - a person with authority to accept the risk for the objective it affects. It needs a rationale that connects the exposure to the objective and shows why the benefit of pursuing the objective outweighs the exposure. It needs a boundary: what specifically is being accepted, for how long, and under what conditions it must be revisited. And it needs a monitoring arrangement, so that acceptance is revisited when the exposure changes rather than standing indefinitely.

This is where risk appetite enters, and the distinction between appetite and tolerance matters. Appetite is the board's overall stance on risk - the amount of risk the organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of objectives, expressed in a form that can guide decisions rather than a form that cannot be applied to any particular decision. Tolerance is the amount of risk that can be tolerated for a specific objective, risk or process, typically expressed in a measurable form such as a threshold, a limit or a service level. A good organisation translates a strategic appetite statement into operational tolerances, and those tolerances into the criteria that a business proposal is tested against.

The practical test of an appetite statement: put it in front of a business unit leader with a real proposal in hand and see whether it produces a decision. If the statement is aspirational and untestable - for example, that the organisation is prudent in its approach to risk - it is decoration. If it is specific enough to rule something in or out, it is an instrument.

A note on acceptance and appetite: accepting a risk that sits outside appetite is a governance event, not a management one. It requires escalation to the level that set the appetite. If the organisation routinely accepts risks outside appetite without escalation, then the appetite statement is not the organisation's real appetite, and reporting to the board on the basis of that statement is misleading.
bullets: Acceptance requires: named acceptor, rationale, boundary and time limit, monitoring arrangement
Appetite is the board's stance; tolerance is the operational threshold for a specific risk
Accepting a risk outside appetite is an escalation event, not a management decision
An appetite statement that cannot rule a decision in or out is not usable
sections.callout: The single most common audit finding in this area is acceptance without an acceptor. If nobody signed, nobody decided.

sections.heading: Is the risk register alive?
sections.body:
A risk register is the most manufactured artefact in the discipline, and most registers in most organisations are dead. The symptoms are recognisable: it is owned by the risk function rather than by the business; it is a spreadsheet of several hundred rows that nobody has reviewed since it was populated; risk descriptions say things like there is a risk of cyber attack; the ratings have not changed in three years even though the organisation has; and there is no link between the register and the decisions the business actually makes.

A live register has a specific character. Each entry states a cause, an objective it threatens, a consequence, a named owner who is a business leader rather than the risk team, and a treatment or acceptance decision with a date. Entries are reviewed on a cycle, and entries disappear when the risk is no longer relevant - a register that only grows is not being managed. Crucially, entries connect to the rest of the governance machinery: to controls, to audit findings, to incidents, to capital and project decisions, to third-party assessments.

Two design choices materially improve register quality. The first is the risk cause formulation - describing the underlying reason the risk exists rather than the event. A good cause is something you can act on: our third-party onboarding process does not include a security assessment. A bad event description is something you can only watch: our third-party might be breached. The second is separating the register by level: a short top-level set of enterprise risks for the board, and detailed underlying risk exposures below, so the board pack is not a hundred rows of heat map.

The last test is the most damning. Ask a business unit leader to name a decision in the last six months where the risk register changed what they did. If they cannot, the register is reporting, not managing.
bullets: Owners are business leaders, not the risk function
Entries state causes and consequences, not just events
Entries are added and removed as the organisation changes
Every entry connects to a treatment or a documented acceptance
A short enterprise level sits above a detailed underlying level
The register demonstrably influenced at least one business decision recently

examples.title: Third-party risk in a telecom operator
examples.context: A mobile network operator places its customer billing and identity services with a cloud provider. Following a near-miss at a different operator, the CRO asks for a specific position on the risk from the cloud provider. The first line business owner says the provider is tier one and has a signed security addendum. The risk register entry reads: risk of third-party outage causing loss of revenue to the enterprise, rated high, with no treatment plan and no named acceptor.
examples.outcome: The GRC analyst reconstructs the entry as a cause-based statement: our dependency on a single provider for a revenue-critical service with no tested exit path. Risk is decomposed into availability, security, regulatory and concentration dimensions, each with a treatment option. Modify (dual-provider design, contractual exit terms) is proposed for concentration and contractual risk; share (insurance) is rejected as ineffective against systemic provider failure; the residual concentration risk is recommended for formal acceptance by the accountable executive because full exit capability is judged disproportionate to the exposure. That recommendation is what a live register enables, and it is exactly what the original entry could not support.

examples.title: Risk appetite in a manufacturer
examples.context: An industrial manufacturer with plants in three countries must set a risk appetite statement for the board. The draft produced by the risk team reads: the company is prudent in its approach to operational and safety risk and will not accept any risk to the safety of employees or the integrity of the environment. Operations respond that this is meaningless because it provides no threshold for, say, a chemical plant operating beyond design limits during a supply shortage.
examples.outcome: The GRC team converts the aspiration into tolerances: zero tolerance for operating a plant outside certified process safety limits; a defined maximum number of days a critical spares line may run with a single-source dependency; and a heat mapping with named escalation for safety and environmental events regardless of financial value. Each tolerance is expressed so that a plant manager can apply it without seeking permission, and so that an exception requires a named senior approver with a time limit. The board can then approve an appetite statement that actually rules decisions in and out, which is the point of the exercise.

practicalExercise.title: Rebuild one risk entry the way a practitioner would
practicalExercise.brief: Take a single risk from a real or hypothetical organisation and rebuild it properly: cause-based statement, objective linkage, likelihood and impact using a documented scale, control assessment, residual risk, appetite comparison and a treatment decision with a named acceptor. You will discover which parts of the original were assumptions.
steps: Write the original risk entry as it is typically recorded. Note every element it omits.
Reformulate it as a cause statement linked to a specific business objective and a named consequence, and state what uncertainty remains.
Define a five-point likelihood scale and a five-point impact scale with written anchors for a chosen business unit, and rate the risk using only those anchors.

List the controls you believe are in place, then mark each as evidenced, partially evidenced or unevidenced based on what you could actually see. Recalculate residual risk using only the evidenced controls.
Compare residual risk with an appetite position you have written, and choose a treatment option. Record the acceptor, the boundary, the review date and the monitoring indicator.
Write a 150-word narrative suitable for inclusion in a board risk report, including the assumption you have made about control effectiveness.
practicalExercise.deliverable: A single-page risk entry in practitioner form, plus a 150-word board-facing narrative that names its key assumption.
evaluationCriteria: The risk statement describes a cause and an objective rather than a feared event
Likelihood and impact are rated against written anchors rather than by instinct, and the anchors are shown
Control effectiveness is distinguished between asserted and evidenced, and residual risk reflects only evidenced controls
The treatment option is one of modify, avoid, share or accept, and the choice is justified against the alternatives
The acceptance decision, if any, names an acceptor, a boundary, a review date and a monitoring indicator
The narrative is readable by a non-specialist board member and states its assumption explicitly

references: ISO 31000:2018, Risk management - Guidelines, Clauses 5, 6 and 8 (Frameworks, Process, Treatment) and Clause 4.4.1 on risk appetite
COSO Enterprise Risk Management: Integrating with Strategy and Performance (2017), 20 principles across five dimensions
ISO/IEC 27005:2022, Information security risk management - Guidelines
NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1, Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments (September 2012)
HM Treasury, The Orange Book: Management of Risk - Principles and Concepts (2023)
UK Government, Orange Book and Red Book (source code risk management guidance)

items.title: What Compliance Actually Means
items.summary: Compliance is the state of meeting obligations, not the activity of reading regulations. This lesson separates law, regulation, standards, codes, policy and contractual obligation; explains how a compliance universe is built and prioritised; covers the compliance risk cycle from obligation identification to testing and reporting; and sets out why compliance and risk are different disciplines that must nonetheless connect.
objectives: Distinguish legal, regulatory, normative, contractual and internal obligations and the consequences of each
Describe how a compliance universe is built, deduplicated and prioritised by exposure
Apply the compliance risk cycle from obligation identification through to testing and reporting
Explain the relationship between compliance and risk management, including where they conflict and why that is normal

sections.heading: Compliance is a state, not a department
sections.body:
Compliance is the condition of conforming to an obligation. The activity of maintaining that condition is compliance management. The confusion matters because organisations consistently structure themselves around the activity - a compliance function, a compliance calendar, a compliance officer - and then assume the state follows. It does not. Compliance is a state that must be evidenced continuously, and it is lost silently - there is no alarm when a contractual notice period lapses.

The obligations themselves come from several sources with genuinely different characteristics, and treating them identically is a common and expensive mistake.

Law and regulation are binding requirements enforced by the state: statutes, regulations, supervisory expectations. Failure usually carries sanctions, and sometimes personal consequences for individuals. The response to law is obedience; the analysis question is what the obligation actually requires in practice, which is rarely a direct restatement of the text.

Codes and standards are usually not law in themselves, but they become law by incorporation, by reference in a contract, or by the fact that a regulator expects them. ISO standards become binding when a regulation names them or when a customer contract does. The treatment of standards must therefore be conditional - applicable because of X - and that condition must be recorded.

Contractual and other commitments - customer and supplier agreements, licences, warranties, industry schemes, internal policies - are binding too, and often less visible than legislation. A missed service credit under a customer contract is a compliance failure that will never appear in a regulatory filing but will appear in a renewal negotiation.

Internal policy is the organisation's own rule. It is binding on staff and is the basis on which many internal controls operate, but it is not a compliance obligation to an external party - which matters when you are prioritising remediation effort.
bullets: Law and regulation: binding, state-enforced, sanctioned; analysis needed to translate into operational requirement
Codes and standards: binding only through incorporation, contract or regulatory expectation; record the basis
Contractual commitments: binding and often invisible in regulatory reporting
Internal policy: binding on staff, supports controls, but is not an external compliance obligation
Obligation source determines the response, the evidence required and the escalation route
sections.callout: Record the basis of applicability for every obligation. A standard is only mandatory because something makes it so - and that something changes over time.

sections.heading: Building the compliance universe
sections.body:
The compliance universe is the complete set of obligations that apply to the organisation, mapped to owners, controls and evidence. Building it is unglamorous work and it is the foundation of everything else. Getting it wrong produces two symmetric failures: obligations that are missed entirely, and obligations that are tracked but not actually applicable, which drains remediation capacity and destroys credibility.

A workable method proceeds in stages. Start with the sources: the regulatory perimeter (which regulators have jurisdiction over which activities, entities and data), the legal entity structure, the product and service catalogue, the market and geography footprint, and the licence and accreditation register. Then map each obligation to an owner in the business - not to the compliance function - because obligations attach to the activity that creates the exposure.

Normalise and deduplicate at this point. Obligations arrive from many directions with overlapping subject matter; a data protection obligation may appear in sector regulation, in a group policy and in a customer contract. A naive universe will contain the same obligation three times with three owners and no single view of the requirement. Group by obligation subject, record every source, and designate one owner.

Then classify by obligation type and consequence. A minor reporting obligation with a small penalty and a payment data protection obligation with a percentage-of-turnover sanction should never sit in the same queue. Prioritisation must combine consequence, likelihood of failure and the difficulty of remediation.

Finally, connect the universe to the rest of the GRC system. Every obligation should point to the control that satisfies it and the evidence that demonstrates it. This is the point at which the compliance universe stops being a legal document exercise and starts being the backbone of an assurance programme - because the same evidence usually satisfies a control assessment, an audit test and a regulatory return.
table: Missing a regulator or a dormant entity
Raw obligation register from every source
One row per obligation with all sources listed
Every obligation owned by the compliance team
Obligation to control and evidence mapping
Uniform effort across trivial and existential items

sections.heading: The compliance risk cycle
sections.body:
A mature compliance function runs a cycle, not a queue. The cycle is: identify obligations; assess the compliance risk inherent in each; design and implement controls; test the controls and the underlying activity; report; and respond to failures with corrective action.

The testing step is where most organisations are weakest, and it is where the discipline either becomes real or becomes theatre. Testing must address both the control (is it designed properly and operating?) and the outcome (did the underlying obligation actually get met?). Testing a control but not the outcome produces assurance about a mechanism rather than about the obligation, and a perfectly designed and perfectly operated control can still fail because the underlying law changed or because the activity produces data the control does not cover.

There are three common testing approaches, and a good programme uses all three in proportion to risk. Self-assessment, where the business owner confirms compliance against a questionnaire, is cheap and covers breadth but is prone to optimism and to copying the previous year. Independent testing, where a second or third line function tests a sample, is stronger evidence and is what regulators and certification bodies expect for higher-risk obligations. And continuous monitoring, where system-generated data substitutes for attestation, is the most scalable and the most objective - payroll data reconciles leave records, payment system logs reconcile card transactions, access review exports reconcile entitlement lists.

Reporting completes the cycle. Compliance reporting should not simply state that obligations were met. It should state which obligations were tested, at what depth, on what sample, what the results were, and where assurance is missing. That last element - coverage transparency - is what allows a board to ask intelligent questions, and it is rarely provided.
bullets: Identify: capture obligations from every source and normalise them
Assess: rate inherent compliance risk per obligation
Control: design and implement, with evidence requirements defined up front
Test: test both the control and the outcome, using self-assessment, independent testing and continuous monitoring in proportion to risk
Report: state what was tested, at what depth, and where assurance is missing
Respond: corrective action on failures, tracked to closure with evidence
sections.callout: A compliance report that gives a percentage compliance rate without stating testing coverage is close to meaningless. Ask for the denominator and the sample.

sections.heading: Compliance and risk: different disciplines, connected system
sections.body:
Compliance and risk management are frequently presented as rivals, usually in the context of a budget argument. They are better understood as two disciplines with different primary questions that must nonetheless share a data model.

Risk management asks: what could prevent us achieving our objectives, and what are we doing about it? It is forward-looking, probabilistic and opportunity-aware. Compliance asks: are we meeting the obligations that apply to us? It is obligation-driven, largely binary in outcome, and concerned with the state of the organisation rather than the trajectory.

The two connect in specific, practical ways. Obligations inform the risk assessment: the likelihood of failing a strict obligation is a real risk input, and in some cases the obligation defines the risk appetite boundary. Risks inform compliance prioritisation: the obligations with the greatest risk consequence deserve the testing depth. Controls serve both: a well-designed access control satisfies a security obligation and reduces an insider threat risk simultaneously.

The genuine conflicts are structural, not conceptual, and recognising them helps you manage the arguments rather than win them. Compliance asks for the control to exist and be evidenced; risk asks whether the control is proportionate to the exposure and affordable. Compliance treats the obligation as fixed; risk asks whether a residual exposure can be accepted and who accepts it. Compliance reporting is binary and comparative across obligations; risk reporting is continuous and comparative across exposure.

The resolution in a mature organisation is a single set of facts used twice. One control testing programme. One risk register that records compliance consequences as impacts. One issue and action system. When these are separate, the organisation is doing the same testing twice and still cannot answer a board question that requires both.

One warning for the practitioner. Never let a risk acceptance become a compliance failure. Accepting a risk is a legitimate decision within appetite; it is not a legitimate response to an obligation. If the residual exposure means we will breach a regulatory requirement, the answer is to fix it, or to stop the activity - not to accept the risk. That distinction should be explicit in any risk acceptance form.
bullets: Risk is forward-looking and probabilistic; compliance asks about a present obligation and a state
Obligations feed the risk assessment; risk consequence informs compliance prioritisation
One control testing programme, one evidence base, two reports drawn from it
Accepting risk never discharges a legal or contractual obligation
Compliance is usually a constraint on treatment options, not one option among many
sections.callout: If someone proposes accepting the risk of breaching a regulatory requirement, the correct response is not escalation. It is to fix it or stop the activity.

examples.title: The obligation that only appears in a customer contract
examples.context: A government IT services provider must meet contractual service levels that are stricter than anything in regulation: a 99.95 per cent uptime commitment with service credits, and a 30-day mandatory data deletion period on contract exit. The compliance universe, built from legislation and regulatory guidance, contains neither. The contract is managed by the commercial team. A contract renewal exposes the organisation to a claim it did not know it had accepted.
examples.outcome: The GRC team adds a contractual obligation source to the universe and a specific obligation type for customer and supplier commitments, with the commercial team as owner. The two commitments are mapped to the existing monitoring controls - uptime measured by the service management platform and a configurable deletion workflow - with evidence retained for audit. The organisation now holds a single register of obligations across law, regulation, contract and policy, and the GRC function can report on coverage across all four rather than only the first two. The lesson reinforced here: the commercial function is an obligation-generating function like any other, and the register must reach it.

examples.title: Reconciling a compliance backlog with a risk-based programme
examples.context: A healthcare provider has 340 obligations in its register, of which 96 have no control linkage and no test coverage. The compliance function proposes a three-year remediation programme costing roughly two million. The risk function argues that most of these obligations carry low consequence and that money would be better spent on two high-impact clinical system risks. The CFO asks the GRC lead to resolve it.
examples.outcome: The GRC lead does not choose between the two disciplines; she merges them. Obligations are re-prioritised by a combination of consequence and failure likelihood rather than by an arbitrary tier, producing four groups: high-consequence obligations needing immediate control work, high-consequence obligations needing independent testing only, low-consequence obligations satisfied by continuous monitoring, and a residual group of legacy obligations consolidated into a single annual attestation. The investment is redirected toward the two high-impact clinical risks, and the compliance backlog shrinks because it was prioritised rather than merely large. The board is shown one programme with two lenses, and the compliance and risk functions now report into the same management review.

practicalExercise.title: Build a compliance universe for a small organisation
practicalExercise.brief: Construct a compliance universe for a fictional mid-sized organisation in a sector of your choice, using a fictional profile rather than a real company. The point of the exercise is to see how obligations arise from multiple sources, how they normalise, and how they connect to controls and evidence.
steps: Define the organisation: sector, revenue scale, geography, number of legal entities, products or services, customer mix, and the data it holds. Write this as a one-page profile.

List the regulatory perimeter: which regulators have jurisdiction, over which entities and activities, and roughly how many obligations each regime typically generates. Estimate a count and note your uncertainty.

Capture at least fifteen specific obligations across at least four source types: legislation, regulation or supervisory guidance, an industry code or standard, a customer or supplier contract, and internal policy.
Normalise: identify any obligations that appear more than once under different names, merge them into one row with multiple sources, and assign a single business owner to each merged row.
Link each obligation to the control that satisfies it and to the evidence that would demonstrate it. Flag any obligation with no linkage.

Classify each obligation by consequence and by testing approach you would use (self-assessment, independent testing, continuous monitoring), and produce a prioritised shortlist of the top five for the first year.
practicalExercise.deliverable: A compliance universe extract with a header describing the organisation, fifteen or more normalised obligations with source, owner, control, evidence and priority, and a one-paragraph note on the two gaps you consider most serious.
evaluationCriteria: Obligations are drawn from at least four different source types and the source is named for each
Normalisation genuinely merges overlapping obligations rather than duplicating them, with all sources retained
Every obligation has a business owner, and the owners are plausibly different people with different responsibilities
Control linkage and evidence are specified for each obligation, and unlinked obligations are explicitly flagged rather than omitted
Prioritisation reflects consequence and testing approach rather than merely listing everything as high priority
Counts and estimates are honest about being estimates rather than implying research that was not performed

ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clause 4.2 (needs and expectations of interested parties) and Clause 6.1 (legal and regulatory requirements)
ISO 19600:2021, Compliance management systems - Guidelines for assessing compliance with law
COSO Enterprise Risk Management: Integrating with Strategy and Performance (2017)
Financial Action Task Force, International Standards on Combating Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism (2012, updated)
Bank for International Settlements, Principles for the Sound Management of Operational Risk (revised March 2021)

items.title: Information Security vs Cybersecurity
items.summary: Information security and cybersecurity overlap heavily but are not interchangeable, and the difference matters for scope, standards and how you talk to the business. This lesson sets out the scope of each, what sits outside both, why the distinction drives different regulatory regimes and different standards, and how to run a sensible conversation when a board conflates them.
objectives: Define information security and cybersecurity and explain where their scopes overlap and diverge
Identify activity that is neither - including safety, privacy and business continuity - and place it correctly
Explain how the distinction changes which standards, laws and metrics apply to a given system
Handle the board-level confusion about the two terms without being pedantic

sections.heading: Two scopes, one problem space
sections.body:
The two terms are frequently used interchangeably, and in practice the work overlaps so heavily that the distinction can seem academic. It is not academic, because the distinction determines scope of standards, which regulators apply, what gets measured, and where the accountability sits.

Information security is the protection of information assets against threats to confidentiality, integrity, availability and authenticity - regardless of the technology involved. It is broader in medium and broader in threat: it covers paper records, physical safeguards, physical tampering, human error, insider misuse, and the paper process by which an invoice is approved. ISO/IEC 27001 is an information security standard. It defines its scope by information and by risk, not by network.

Cybersecurity is the narrower, technology-centred discipline concerned with the protection of connected systems, networks, devices, applications and data in the digital environment. Its scope is defined by the attack surface and the adversary. NIST SP 800-53 and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework are the reference points, and both are explicitly framed around information systems and the threats to them.

The overlap is where the work actually happens - the majority of control activity sits in both. The divergence shows in three places. First, medium: information security includes physical and paper controls; cybersecurity is by definition digital. Second, threat model: information security includes insider abuse, human error, process failure and physical compromise; cybersecurity concentrates on external and technically sophisticated adversaries. Third, organisational ownership: in many organisations the CISO owns cybersecurity and a separate information governance or records function owns the policy and standards side of information security.

The practical consequence is that a control implemented for information security purposes may be entirely outside a cybersecurity framework. A clean-desk policy, a physical destruction register, a supplier audit of paper-based processes - all legitimate information security controls, all invisible to a cybersecurity dashboard.
bullets: Information security: protects information assets across all media and all threat types, including physical, human and process
Cybersecurity: protects connected systems, networks and devices against digital threats
Overlap is large and covers most technical control activity
Divergence appears in medium, threat model and often in organisational ownership
Physical and paper controls are information security controls that a cybersecurity framework will never capture
table: Systems, networks and the digital attack surface
All media, including paper and physical
Digital systems and the data on them
External, internal, human error, physical, process failure
Adversarial and technical attacks, malware, exploitation
Control operating effectiveness, incident and breach rates by asset
Coverage of the attack surface, mean time to detect, patch latency

sections.heading: What sits outside both
sections.body:
Three adjacent disciplines are frequently pulled into information security conversations because they share people, systems and incidents, but they have their own objectives, standards and accountability.

Safety and operational resilience cover the physical harm and the continuity of a process. A chemical plant's safety case, a hospital's clinical safety obligations and an airline's operational safety management are not information security problems, even though a compromised control system can cause physical harm. The management of that interface - safety and security - is a distinct and increasingly important discipline, and confusing it with either information security or cybersecurity is a common root cause of poorly governed OT and IoT environments.

Privacy is about the lawful processing of personal information - the individual's rights, the lawful basis, transparency, minimisation, retention and transfer. It shares infrastructure and often shares the CISO, and it has its own regime (GDPR, UK GDPR, and sector privacy law) and its own standards (ISO/IEC 27701, NIST Privacy Framework). An access control can serve both, but a privacy obligation can arise where no security control would: the lawful basis for processing, a retention period, a data subject request response. Conflating the two leads to security teams being asked to explain the lawful basis for processing, which they cannot, and privacy teams being asked to approve a firewall rule, which they should not.

Business continuity and resilience cover the ability to keep delivering critical services. Backup, disaster recovery and service restoration plans sit here, and so does much of what a CISO is accountable for - which is why the boundary is often contested. A useful division: information security owns protecting the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information assets; resilience owns ensuring the business can continue to operate, using information security and other controls as one of several inputs.

Legal hold, records management and litigation readiness sit in a fourth bucket. They impose obligations on the organisation to preserve information, which can directly conflict with deletion or modification obligations, and the reconciliation is a legal rather than a technical task.
bullets: Safety and operational resilience: physical harm and process continuity, including OT and IoT
Privacy: lawful processing and individual rights, with its own legal regime and standards
Business continuity and resilience: keeping critical services operating, using security controls as one input
Records, legal hold and litigation readiness: preservation obligations that can conflict with deletion
sections.callout: A useful referral rule: if the question is who is allowed to see it or why it was collected, it is privacy. If it is who can change it, steal it or destroy it, it is information security. If it is how fast we can get it back, it is resilience.

sections.heading: Why the distinction changes what you must do
sections.body:
The practical consequence of the scoping difference is that the same organisation can be simultaneously compliant with one framework and non-compliant with another, with no contradiction.

Consider a hospital. Under ISO/IEC 27001, the ISMS scope follows the information and the risk - so the medical imaging archive, the pathology reporting system, the paper referral process and the patient administration system are all candidates, and controls such as physical media handling and clean-desk practice belong in scope. Under a cybersecurity framework focused on the IT estate, the imaging archive might be in scope as a system while the paper process is not, and the paper controls appear nowhere in the results. A board that receives a green cybersecurity dashboard and assumes green coverage of information security is being misled by a definitional boundary.

The distinction also drives regulatory mapping. NIS2 and equivalent regimes are framed around essential and important entities and their digital infrastructure, obligations such as risk management measures, incident reporting and supply chain security. Data protection regimes are framed around processing of personal data. A medical device manufacturer's obligations may sit under medical device regulation, which in the EU is the Cyber Resilience Act, requiring security-by-design and vulnerability handling for products with digital elements. Each regime has its own scope, its own reporting clock and its own supervisory body. Managing them coherently requires a map from obligation to system, not a single framework.

Finally, the distinction shapes what you measure. Cybersecurity metrics concentrate on adversary-facing activity: vulnerability counts, patch latency, detection coverage, phishing click rates. Information security metrics concentrate on the control system as a whole: policy currency, access review completion, incident handling by asset class, third-party assurance coverage. Neither metric set answers the question the other was designed for.
bullets: The same organisation can be compliant with one framework and non-compliant with another without contradiction
Sector regimes such as NIS2, DORA and the EU Cyber Resilience Act define their own scope and reporting obligations
Different frameworks drive different metrics; a cybersecurity dashboard does not evidence information security coverage
Board reporting must state which scope the reported results cover

sections.heading: Handling the conversation when the terms are conflated
sections.body:
In practice you will rarely get the luxury of a definitional discussion. Boards use the words loosely, and correcting a director pedantically is a poor use of your time. What you can do is make the scope explicit in the artefacts, so that the conflation stops mattering.

The technique is to make scope a labelled field rather than an implied assumption. Every framework, register, assessment and report states what it covers and what it excludes. The policy set is indexed by scope. The risk register entries reference the framework they were assessed against. The security dashboard states its coverage boundary - which sites, which systems, which business lines - in the same visual block as the numbers.

The second technique is to answer the board's actual question. Directors rarely care about the taxonomy; they care about whether the organisation is exposed and whether they are being told the truth. A good answer is: here is what we protect and how we know it is protected; here is what is not covered by this view, and here is what we do about that; here is the summary of exposure across everything, including the parts outside the technical scope.

The third technique is to be honest about the seam. Where information security and cybersecurity are owned by different people - which is very common - the risk is not the boundary itself, it is the gap in coverage at the boundary. Physical security managed by facilities, records and archive managed by the corporate secretary, OT managed by operations. A good GRC review tests the seams explicitly rather than assuming that coverage is uniform.

Finally, do not weaponise the distinction. When a director says cybersecurity when they mean information security, they are not making a philosophical error, they are asking a question they need answered. Answer the question and note the scope difference once, in writing, in the pack, and move on.
bullets: Make scope an explicit labelled field in every framework, register and report
Answer the board's underlying question - exposure and truthfulness - rather than the taxonomy
Test the seams where ownership splits: physical security, records, OT, facilities
Note the distinction once in writing and continue; do not relitigate terminology in the room
sections.callout: The question behind almost every scope dispute is: is there a part of the organisation that nobody is looking at? Answer that, and the taxonomy stops being interesting.

examples.title: A green dashboard over an uncovered hospital estate
examples.context: A hospital network's board receives a monthly security dashboard showing a 99.2 per cent phishing simulation failure rate, a patch compliance figure of 97 per cent, and zero high-severity incidents. The board concludes the hospital is well protected. Meanwhile, the information governance team has just handled a serious incident in which paper referral letters including patient identifiers were found in an unsecured recycling bin in an outpatient building managed by a facilities contractor.
examples.outcome: The GRC lead adds a scope statement to the dashboard and a second panel covering the managed estate: physical records handling, contractor controls, paper-based workflows and the information security management system coverage of those processes. The board's conclusion is corrected, not by argument but by giving them the view they were missing. The follow-up is an information security assessment of the paper estate and a control set for physical media destruction - none of which the cybersecurity programme would ever have produced. The incident also becomes a case study in why a single framework dashboard cannot answer an enterprise assurance question.

examples.title: Regulatory scope collisions in a telecom operator
examples.context: A telecom operator is subject to NIS2, to national critical infrastructure requirements, to data protection law, and to a sector regulator's outsourcing and resilience rules. The GRC lead is asked to produce a single assurance plan. Each regime defines scope slightly differently, one includes the radio access network, another excludes certain wholesale functions, and the reporting clocks and thresholds differ.
examples.outcome: Rather than forcing a single control set, the lead builds an obligation-to-control-to-evidence map keyed by the smallest common denominator of scope - the operational technology estate, the customer-facing platforms and the corporate systems - and then attaches the regime-specific requirements as overlays. One testing programme serves all four regimes, but each regulatory return is assembled from the same evidence with regime-specific thresholds, timelines and escalation paths recorded against it. The board sees one enterprise assurance view; the regulators each receive what they are entitled to, on time, with traceability back to a single control testing record.

practicalExercise.title: Scope an organisation and find the seams
practicalExercise.brief: Define the information security scope of an organisation of your choosing, then draw the cybersecurity scope separately, and identify the material difference between the two. Finish by identifying the places where ownership splits - the seams - and stating who is accountable for each.
steps: Describe the organisation: sectors, sites, systems, data types, workforce profile and any physical or paper-based processes.

Write the information security scope: everything whose compromise could harm the organisation, regardless of medium. Include physical records, archives, telephone records, printed reports and any process run by a contractor on paper or on your hardware.
Write the cybersecurity scope: the connected systems, the estate under your networks and cloud identities, the internet-facing and internal attack surface, and the data on those systems.
List what appears in the first list and not the second, and what appears in the second and not the first. Explain why each difference exists.
Draw the seams: where does ownership change hands - facilities, records, OT, HR, legal, outsourced providers - and identify who owns information security for each seam.
Write a 120-word scope statement for a board pack that states what is covered, what is not, and the plan for the not-covered parts.
practicalExercise.deliverable: A one-page scope document with two scope definitions, a difference list with explanations, a seam map with named owners, and a board-facing scope paragraph.
evaluationCriteria: The information security scope includes non-digital media and physical processes, not just IT systems
The cybersecurity scope is defined by systems and attack surface rather than by department
Differences between the two scopes are explained rather than merely listed
Seams are identified with an accountable owner for each, not left as general statements about contractors
The board-facing statement is plain English, states the boundary honestly, and commits to a plan for uncovered areas
