items.title: GRC Operating Models
items.summary: An operating model decides who does what work, in what sequence, with what technology and under what incentives - and it determines whether the GRC function is a control or a decoration. This lesson covers the main operating model archetypes for GRC (federated, centralised, hybrid, centralised-outsourced and product operating model), the trade-offs each creates, and how to design one that actually changes behaviour.
objectives: Describe the main GRC operating model archetypes and the trade-offs each creates
Assess a given operating model against the three questions that determine whether it works: clarity of accountability, capacity, and incentive alignment
Identify the failure modes that appear when a GRC operating model is designed around reporting rather than decision support
Design an operating model for a specified organisation and justify the choices made

sections.heading: What an operating model actually is
sections.body:
An operating model is the answer to a set of practical questions: who does the work, in what sequence, with what information, using what tools, under what incentives, and with what accountability when it goes wrong. Structure charts answer only the first. Most organisations over-invest in structure and under-invest in the rest, which is why reorganisations frequently fail to change behaviour.

For GRC specifically, six design questions recur. Scope: which activities and which parts of the enterprise are in the GRC remit, and which are explicitly out? Right-sizing: which of the three lines does each activity belong to, in line with the IIA Three Lines Model? Capacity: does the function have the people, skills and budget to do the work it owns? Rhythm: what is the cadence - daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, annual - and which decisions attach to which forum? Instrumentation: which systems hold the facts, and which are used to decide and record? And incentives: what is each role measured and rewarded on, in practice rather than in the objectives statement?

The last question is the one that decides whether the model works. An organisation where first-line managers are measured on revenue and cost, and separately on risk metrics that are not connected to either, will get the behaviour that is rewarded. Governance design that ignores this produces policies that are approved, published, ignored and then cited as evidence of failure by an auditor.

A good operating model also answers a question that structure charts never do: how does a risk or issue get from where it is detected to where it can be decided? Most models describe reporting lines and no decision path, and then complain that escalation is slow. The path should be explicit: detection point, decision maker, threshold, timeframe, and what happens if the timeframe is missed.
bullets: Scope: what is in and out of the GRC remit
Right-sizing: which line does each activity belong to
Capacity: people, skills and budget against the work owned
Rhythm: cadence of reviews and the decisions attached to each
Instrumentation: where the facts live and where decisions are recorded
Incentives: what roles are actually measured and rewarded on
sections.callout: The test of an operating model: describe the behaviour it produces in a scenario where the incentives and the rules conflict. That behaviour is your real operating model.

sections.heading: The main GRC operating model archetypes
sections.body:
Five patterns cover most of the organisations you will meet. None is universally right, and hybrid approaches dominate in practice.

The federated model places a small central function that sets policy, defines the framework and provides tooling and assurance, with the substance of the work - risk identification, control operation, compliance monitoring - sitting in business units and country entities. This suits large multinationals with genuinely different local contexts, and it scales well. Its characteristic failure is drift: local interpretations of the central policy multiply until the framework is no longer comparable across the enterprise, and the centre is reduced to publishing guidance nobody reads.

The centralised model consolidates the majority of GRC work in a single centre, typically with shared services handling process execution and reporting. This creates consistency, professional standards and a single data model, and it is efficient at scale for process-oriented work. Its failure is distance: the people doing the work do not know the business, and the business does not feel the work as theirs. Risk registers become the centre's document rather than the business's instrument, and the centre becomes a bottleneck that people route around. It also concentrates key-person risk and produces fragility.

The hybrid model - by far the most common - centres certain activities and distributes others. The typical pattern: central ownership of policy, methodology, taxonomy, the risk appetite framework and consolidated reporting; local ownership of risk identification, control operation and first-line compliance activity; a shared services layer for transactional execution; independent second and third line functions at the centre. The design work is in deciding exactly where the line falls, and in making the interfaces explicit rather than implicit.

The centralised-outsourced model outsources substantial execution to a provider, typically with the internal function retaining methodology, standard setting, quality assurance and the supplier relationship. This can work extremely well for high-volume, well-defined processes such as control testing, issue management administration or regulatory reporting. The characteristic failure is the hollow centre: the internal team retains the accountability but loses the practical knowledge, so the provider does the thinking and the internal function cannot challenge the provider's work when it goes wrong.

The product operating model treats GRC as an internal product delivered to the business, with a roadmap, a service catalogue, defined service levels and user feedback. This is a genuinely useful framing because it forces you to define what you deliver and to whom, and it makes prioritisation a product decision rather than a political one. Its failure mode is commoditisation: if the product team only serves internal business units, they can end up optimising for the requests of the loudest stakeholder rather than the enterprise's risk priorities. It needs an explicit enterprise mandate and a governance route for prioritisation.
table: Consistency, single data model, scale efficiency
GRC as an internal service function

sections.heading: The three questions that decide whether it works
sections.body:
Whatever the archetype, an operating model can be stress-tested against three questions. If it fails any of them, no amount of organisational design polish will rescue it.

The first is accountability clarity. For every significant GRC output - a risk position, a compliance conclusion, a control assurance result, an audit finding - can you name one person accountable for it? Failsafes matter more than is usually acknowledged here: in a matrixed model, work frequently has two owners who each assume the other is covering the gap. Where accountability is genuinely shared, the practice that works is to split it explicitly into producing the output and challenging it, rather than leaving both to a single vague mandate.

The second is capacity fit. Compare the work the model asks for against the people and budget available, and do the arithmetic honestly. A risk register reviewed quarterly for 400 risks by a team of four, each risk needing thirty minutes of analysis, is roughly 200 hours per quarter - feasible. The same register with 4,000 risks and annual review cycles is not. Where models are persistently over-committed, the consequence is not that the organisation accepts the shortfall; it is that the assurance outputs get progressively thinner each year while the reporting continues to look complete. Capacity analysis should also cover skills: a second line function staffed entirely by auditors may be excellent at testing and unable to design a risk assessment.

The third is incentive alignment. Take the behaviours the model assumes: first-line managers identifying issues promptly; control owners performing reviews on schedule; business units accepting that a failed control gets escalated. Ask what each role is measured on, and whether a rational person following their scorecard produces the assumed behaviour. Where the answer is no, the model change must precede the expectation, or the expectation must be attached to the scorecard.

The most useful diagnostic question for any operating model is what happens under pressure. When the quarter closes and resources are scarce, what does the organisation actually do first? If the answer is that assurance work is quietly dropped, then the model works only in a world with surplus capacity, and it should be redesigned to specify the minimum viable assurance and the degradation path.
bullets: Accountability clarity: one named accountable owner per significant output, with producing and challenging split where genuinely shared
Capacity fit: arithmetic on volume, effort and budget, plus a skills audit against the work
Incentive alignment: does following the scorecard produce the behaviour the model assumes?
Degradation path: what is dropped first when resources are scarce, and is that decision explicit?
sections.callout: Assurance capacity problems do not surface as a decision. They surface as outputs that get thinner each year while the reporting still looks complete.

sections.heading: Designing an operating model that changes behaviour
sections.body:
Most operating model redesigns fail for a predictable reason: they reorganise boxes and call it done. Behaviour changes only when the redesigned model changes what people do on Monday morning. There are four levers that reliably do that.

The first is workflow. Change the sequence in which work happens and the behaviour changes without anyone resisting. If a risk is now raised by the process owner at the moment a decision is taken rather than collected centrally at quarter end, the register becomes live. If a control failure is now raised automatically by monitoring rather than by a monthly self-assessment, the information improves and the workload moves.

The second is the location of the decision. Push decisions closer to the facts and you get better decisions and faster escalation; push them up and you get consistency and slower response. There is no correct answer, but the decision point should be defined as part of the model, with a threshold, a decision maker and a default action if nobody decides. The default action matters more than people expect - it is what actually happens.

The third is the data model. A single identifier scheme that ties a risk to a control to an obligation to an audit finding to an incident changes behaviour because it makes duplication visible. When a risk and an audit finding can be shown to be the same thing, the argument about whether to raise it separately collapses. Conversely, if the same concept has four identifiers in four systems, the organisation will produce four versions of the truth and argue about them for years.

The fourth is the incentive and consequence structure. Escalation must have consequences, and they must be proportionate. If a failed control triggers no visible response at any level, then the implicit message is that failing controls is costless, and every governance design built on volunteerism will slowly fail.

One warning. Do not redesign the operating model and the framework in the same programme. A methodology change makes people insecure about their judgement, a scope change triggers anxiety about job security, and a tooling change consumes attention. Layering all three at once means that when performance dips, the cause is unattributable and the redesign gets abandoned. Sequence it: establish the data model and the decision paths first, then the structure, then the tools.
bullets: Change workflow and sequence before changing structure
Define decision points with a threshold, a decision maker and a default action
Adopt one identifier scheme that links risk, control, obligation, finding and incident
Give escalation visible consequences that are proportionate and consistently applied
Sequence the programme: data model, then decision paths, then structure, then tooling

examples.title: From central testing to federated assurance in a bank
examples.context: A retail bank with 180 branches and a central second line performs risk and control testing centrally across the whole estate. Testing takes eleven weeks per cycle, findings arrive too late to influence the business year, and the second line is the bottleneck for every request. Branch managers describe the process as an annual inspection that tells them what happened last year.
examples.outcome: The redesign moves the first cycle of testing - risk self-assessment and control walkthroughs - to branch and business-line ownership, with the central function retaining methodology, quality assurance over a sampled subset, escalation of failures and consolidated reporting. The central team's capacity is redeployed to the analytics and thematic reviews it could never get to when it was doing volume testing. The key design decision is a validation layer: the centre samples a fixed percentage of self-assessments and re-performs a fixed number outright, so quality is assured without the centre doing the work. Critical controls - a named minority - remain centrally tested, because the risk of a bad self-assessment on those is unacceptable.

examples.title: A manufacturing GRC function built as an internal product
examples.context: An industrial manufacturer with plants in six countries has a GRC team of nine supporting 4,000 staff. Requests arrive ad hoc by email, senior business leaders escalate directly to the GRC manager, and the team's workload is dominated by whatever shouted loudest last week. Plant managers regard GRC as an obstacle to production.
examples.outcome: The team reframes itself as an internal product with a catalogue: risk assessment support, compliance assurance, control testing, incident analysis, reporting. Each service has a defined audience, a service level, a request intake route and a published scope. Prioritisation is governed: requests are scored against enterprise risk priority and service level, and the steering group approves the roadmap quarterly. Plant managers now have a predictable route to get what they need, and the GRC manager can show the board a service performance report rather than a list of activities. The cultural shift is visible in one number: the proportion of GRC effort spent on the top five enterprise risks rises from under a third to over half within two cycles.

practicalExercise.title: Design a GRC operating model for a specified organisation
practicalExercise.brief: Design a GRC operating model for an organisation of your choosing, with three deliverables: a responsibility map showing what each function does across the three lines, an assessment against the three stress-test questions, and a sequencing plan. The exercise is about making trade-offs explicit, not about producing an organisation chart.
steps: Profile the organisation: size, structure, sectors, number of locations, regulatory load, and the current GRC headcount and budget.

List the twelve to fifteen core GRC activities required (risk identification, appetite setting, control operation, compliance monitoring, internal audit, issue management, reporting, third-party assessment, incident response support and so on) and assign each to first, second or third line with a named function.
Test accountability: for each of the six most significant outputs, name the single accountable owner and state where producing and challenging are split.

Run the capacity calculation: estimate annual effort per activity against available FTE, using stated assumptions, and identify the gap. Then state the degradation path - what is dropped first when capacity is short.
Check incentive alignment for three roles against their actual scorecards. Identify any behaviour the model assumes but the scorecard does not reward.
Write a sequenced plan of no more than five moves, stating what changes first, what changes second, and what you deliberately do not change yet.
practicalExercise.deliverable: A three-part document: a responsibility map across the three lines, a stress-test table covering accountability, capacity and incentives, and a sequenced five-move plan with the reasoning for the order.
evaluationCriteria: Every core activity is assigned to a line with a named function, and the three lines are distinguished by purpose rather than by headcount
Accountability is unambiguous for the six most significant outputs, and shared accountability is explicitly split rather than left vague
The capacity calculation shows its assumptions and produces an honest gap rather than an assertion of feasibility
A degradation path is specified, naming what is dropped first and who decides
The incentive check identifies at least one specific misalignment between an assumed behaviour and an actual scorecard
The sequencing plan explains why each move comes before the next and what is deliberately deferred

ISO 31000:2018 Clause 5.3 (Roles, responsibilities and authorities) and Clause 6.1 (Customisation)
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clause 5.3 (Organizational roles, responsibilities and authorities)
COSO Internal Control: Integrated Framework (2013), Principle 12 and Principle 13 on control activities and deployment
COSO ERM: Integrating with Strategy and Performance (2017), strategy and objective-setting dimension
HM Treasury, The Orange Book: Management of Risk - Principles and Concepts (2023), organisational capacity

items.title: Enterprise Governance Structures and Board Oversight
items.summary: Board oversight is a distinct activity from board decision-making, and it fails in predictable ways when the two are confused. This lesson covers the anatomy of a board and its committees, what effective oversight looks like in practice, the difference between monitoring and challenge, and how to design a board reporting pack that earns its length.
objectives: Describe the anatomy of a board and its committee structure and the purpose each part serves
Distinguish oversight from decision-making and from management reporting, and explain why the distinction affects pack design
Apply the characteristics of effective oversight to a specific board and identify weaknesses
Design or critique the structure of a board reporting pack that supports genuine challenge

sections.heading: The anatomy of board governance
sections.body:
A board is a decision-making body with fiduciary or equivalent duties to the organisation or the people it serves. Everything else about it - the committees, the advisers, the reporting - exists to help the board make good decisions and discharge its duties.

The classic structure is a unitary board (a single board of directors with all responsibilities) or a two-tier structure (a supervisory board overseeing a management board). Many large European organisations, particularly banks and insurers, operate two-tier; most listed companies, and most public sector bodies and private companies, operate unitary. As a GRC professional, the relevant point is that the structure determines who is accountable for management performance - and that accountability is the thing you are often asked to evidence.

The board itself typically delegates three things: the running of the organisation to the executive, the independent assurance of specific areas to committees, and the specialist work of finance, audit, remuneration, nomination and risk to standing committees. The board retains what cannot be delegated: the determination of strategy and objectives, the approval of the risk appetite, the oversight of the control environment, and the accountability for assurance.

Underneath the board sit the executive leadership team and the executive committees that run the business. This is where a lot of GRC professionals spend their time, and it is worth being explicit that executive management committees are not governance structures in the board sense. They are management forums with delegated authority. A useful test for any forum: if its decisions need board ratification, it is not a decision-making forum; if its decisions bind the organisation without ratification, it needs the authority to do so.
bullets: Unitary board: directors carry both oversight and management accountability; two-tier separates a supervisory board from a management board
The board delegates the running of the organisation to the executive and retains accountability for objectives, appetite and the control environment
Standing committees typically cover audit, risk, remuneration and nomination
Executive leadership committees are management forums, not governance structures, unless they hold delegated authority

sections.heading: Oversight is not monitoring, and neither is reporting
sections.body:
Three activities get blurred together in board reporting, and separating them is the single highest-value thing a GRC professional can bring to a board pack.

Monitoring is watching. The organisation measures, tracks and reports. Management does the monitoring; the second and third lines provide independent assurance that the monitoring is accurate and complete. Monitoring is necessary and entirely insufficient.

Oversight is the activity of holding management to account for performance against objectives and for the risk profile they are running. Oversight involves challenge, judgement and a decision to accept, require action, or escalate. It is fundamentally an activity of the board, supported by independent assurance. If a board is only ever shown metrics, it is monitoring, not overseeing - and it will not be able to tell the difference between a well-run risk and a well-presented risk.

Reporting is the transmission of information. Reporting is a means, not an end. A board can receive excellent reporting and still conduct no oversight, because the content does not invite a decision.

Why does this matter practically? Because the design of the pack follows from the purpose. A monitoring pack is a dashboard: trends, against target, with commentary. An oversight pack has a different structure - it presents the position, frames the judgement required, states the options and the recommendation, and identifies the decision the board is being asked to make. If your board pack contains no questions, it is not an oversight pack.

A useful test for the whole system: for each item in the board pack, can you name the decision the board is being asked to make, and what happens if it makes no decision? If the answer is usually nothing, then the item is informational. Boards should receive a large majority of informational items - that is legitimate - but the distinction must be explicit, because it determines whether the board is meeting or watching.
table: Management, with second and third line assurance of the data
The board, supported by independent assurance
A recorded decision with an owner
sections.callout: If no item in the board pack asks the board to decide something, the board is not governing - it is being briefed.

sections.heading: What effective board oversight looks like
sections.body:
Boards with genuinely effective oversight share a set of observable characteristics. They are worth learning as a diagnostic, because most boards believe they have oversight and are actually running a reporting process.

The first characteristic is that the board spends a disproportionate share of its time on the few things that matter. Most boards spend the great majority of time on the easiest material - financial performance, where the variance is small and the story is clear. The genuinely decisive questions - are we inside appetite on this new business line, is our culture capable of sustaining this control environment, are we exposed to a concentration we have not discussed - get the least time.

The second is that the board receives dissent. A board that only ever hears the executive's account, prepared by the executive, will approve what it is given. Mature boards require the second line and the third line to have a direct line to the board or to a board committee without going through the executive, and they require that dissenting views are recorded.

The third is that decisions are tracked. Board decisions on strategy, risk acceptance, remediation and significant investment all generate actions, and a board that does not track its own actions will approve the same remediation twice in consecutive years. The tracking should be visible to the board, not just held in the minutes.

The fourth is that the board understands what it does not know. This is the hardest and the most valuable. Effective boards ask for the assurance gaps to be presented explicitly, and treat a stated gap as a useful contribution rather than a failure to hide.

The fifth is that the board's time is protected and its agenda is designed, not inherited. A board whose agenda is assembled from whatever reports arrived is a board that receives briefing. A board whose agenda is set around a small number of standing strategic questions, with reports slotted into those questions, is a board that governs.

The sixth is that the board's composition matches the risk profile: independent and industry-expert members, appropriate skills, a manageable size, and genuine diversity of challenge rather than of biography. The most common failure is a board that is technically expert in the business but has no member with the standing to challenge on risk and control questions.
bullets: Time concentrates on the few decisions that are genuinely material
The board receives dissent directly from the second and third lines, not only through the executive
Board decisions generate tracked actions visible to the board
Assurance gaps are presented to the board as information, not concealed
The agenda is designed around standing strategic questions rather than inherited from reporting cycles
Composition and skills match the risk profile, including the ability to challenge

sections.heading: Designing a board pack that earns its length
sections.body:
The board pack is the most powerful and most misused artefact in governance. The failure pattern is well known: packs grow, directors read what they can and skim the rest, presenters talk through the pages, and the meeting concludes with a discussion that could have happened without the papers.

The countermeasure is to design backwards from the decisions. Start by listing the decisions the board is being asked to make in the period - typically five to twelve for a quarterly cycle. For each, identify the decision owner, the material options, the recommendation, and the evidence the board needs to exercise judgement. Then build the pack around those, and put everything else in an appendix or a standing information section. The result is a shorter pack that supports real decisions, and a meeting with time to think.

Some specific techniques that consistently improve pack quality. Front-load: the pack opens with the decisions required, each with a recommendation and a clear statement of what the board is being asked to do, not a summary of the last quarter's activity. Use one-page summaries with the detail in an annex, so a director can read the whole pack in thirty minutes and the deep content is still available. State the numbers with their denominator and their basis - a percentage with no base, and a trend with no scale, are the two most common ways packs mislead. Show the exceptions, not the averages: an average that has been stable because two large numbers offset is hiding the only thing the board should see. And put the assurance gaps and the data quality caveats in the pack rather than in the presenter notes, because the caveats are what make the numbers usable.

On the last point, be careful not to overstate. A pack littered with caveats to avoid committing to a view is as useless as a confident pack with no caveats. The right balance is: one clear view, with the specific conditions under which it holds stated once, in plain language.

One further point for a GRC professional: the quality of the board's information is ultimately a function of the organisation's data, not of the pack designer. If the pack is assembled by hand every quarter from six source systems with four different definitions, the problem is upstream. Fixing the definitions and the source integration produces a better pack permanently; reformatting the pack produces a better pack once.
bullets: Design backwards from the decisions the board must make, not from the reporting cycle
Front-load: open with the decisions required and a recommendation for each
One-page summaries with detail in annexes; the whole pack readable in about thirty minutes
Every number with its denominator, basis and comparison point
Show exceptions and outliers explicitly rather than averaging them away
Assurance gaps and data quality caveats in the pack itself, stated once and plainly
Fix the upstream data definitions before optimising the pack layout
sections.callout: A pack that contains no question to the board is a report. A pack that contains a question on every page is a decision agenda. Aim for the second.

examples.title: A board that approved the same remediation twice
examples.context: A mid-sized telecommunications infrastructure company has an audit committee that receives a quarterly pack of approximately ninety pages. Findings are presented with status. The committee approves remediation plans, minuting them accurately. Over the following year, the same two findings - a delayed deprovisioning process and an unreviewed privileged access list - are reported again with modest improvements and again approved. Nobody can identify any decision the committee made in the year that changed anything.
examples.outcome: The GRC lead rebuilds the committee's materials around a tracked decision register: each finding carries a specific, dated commitment and the committee reviews only ageing and escalated items at the meeting, with routine progress moved to a one-page written update. Over two quarters the finding recurrence rate falls sharply, and the committee's agenda shifts from status narration to three live decisions. The deeper fix is institutional: the committee explicitly approves the quarterly decision calendar at the start of the year, so the meeting is planned as a decision forum and the ninety pages become reference material rather than the event.

examples.title: Board oversight of safety in an industrial group
examples.context: An industrial manufacturing group operates chemical plants and a fleet. The group board receives a safety dashboard showing a lost-time injury rate that has improved for six consecutive quarters and a green rating against the group standard. A year later a significant process safety incident occurs at a plant, and the board learns that the dashboard metric had been rebased to exclude contractor injuries - a change made by the operations function without escalation. The board asks how governance failed.
examples.outcome: The review finds that the board had received monitoring rather than oversight: metrics without the underlying definition changes, without leading indicators, and without any mechanism to surface dissent. The redesigned assurance includes definition-change control on every reported metric, a mandatory reporting of any restatement, leading indicators (near-miss rate, overdue safety-critical maintenance, contractor hours on high-risk tasks) alongside lagging indicators, and a standing item for the second line to report directly to the committee. The board also changes its own behaviour: it now requires the CISO and the Chief Risk Officer to brief it on their own assessment rather than the executive's summary, and it asks one question per plant per quarter. The lesson recorded is that metric reliability is a governance matter, not a reporting one.

practicalExercise.title: Critique and redesign a board pack
practicalExercise.brief: Take a board pack you have seen - from your own organisation, a public company, a regulator, or a published annual report - and critique it against the decision-led design standard. Then redesign the opening section so that a director could use it to make a decision in five minutes.
steps: Inventory the pack: list every item, its length, and the reporting cycle it comes from. Identify how many items are metrics, how many are narrative and how many request a decision.
Reconstruct the decisions: list the decisions the board actually made in the last year that you can evidence. Compare against the pack items to find the mismatch.

Test each of five items against the pack-quality criteria: denominator and basis stated, exceptions visible rather than averaged, caveats in the document, recommendation present, decision owner identified.
Write the redesigned opening section: one page, containing the decisions required for the coming quarter, each with a recommendation, the options, and the material evidence.
Produce a one-page change note for the board secretary explaining what you removed, what you moved to appendix and what you added, and what decision-making time you expect to recover.
practicalExercise.deliverable: A critique table across five pack items, a redesigned one-page decision section, and a one-page change note for the board secretary.
evaluationCriteria: The critique identifies the mismatch between decisions actually made and items presented, with evidence
Each tested item is assessed against all five pack-quality criteria, with a specific observation rather than a general comment
The redesigned section contains decisions, not metrics, and each decision has a recommendation, options and a decision owner
Recommendations are stated in plain language and are arguable - a recommendation with no alternative to weigh is not a decision aid
The change note is addressed to the board secretary, is practical, and sets an expectation about decision-making time
The analysis distinguishes problems in the pack from problems in the underlying data, and says which to fix first

items.title: Board Risk Committee, Audit Committee and Risk Committee
items.summary: Board-level committees overlap, and organisations that confuse them produce duplicated effort and unclear accountability. This lesson compares the audit committee, the board risk committee and the management risk committee, covers what each should receive, how memberships are usually composed, and how conflicts between them are resolved in practice.
objectives: Compare the distinct purposes, memberships and reporting lines of the audit committee, board risk committee and management risk committee
Define the content of the standing agenda for each forum and defend the distinction against duplication
Identify the common failure modes in committee design, including overlapping mandates and independence failures
Design a committee structure for a given organisation and resolve a stated conflict between two committees

sections.heading: Why committees exist at all
sections.body:
A board of eight to twelve people cannot give every material matter the sustained attention it needs. Committees exist to concentrate the board's scarce time and expertise on a defined subject area, and to make decisions within a delegated authority so that the full board's agenda is manageable.

Three consequences follow, and they explain most committee design choices. First, a committee is a delegated board - its decisions bind the organisation in the same way board decisions do, which means its terms of reference and quorum rules matter legally and operationally. Second, because a committee sees a narrower slice, it must have a mechanism to inform the whole board of what it did, and the boundary between committee information and board information must be deliberate. Third, committees are where independent challenge is most concentrated, so their membership - particularly independence and the presence of specific expertise - is the design decision that most affects their value.

What committees do not do is absorb the board's accountability. A matter delegated to a committee remains a matter the board is accountable for. If the risk committee cannot get a decision made on a matter because the executive will not accept its recommendation, that is a board escalation, and the terms of reference should say so.
sections.callout: A committee is a delegated board, not a subordinate forum. Its decisions bind the organisation, and the board remains accountable for what it decides.

sections.heading: The audit committee
sections.body:
The audit committee is the board's independent oversight of financial reporting, internal control, internal audit and external audit. In most jurisdictions it is a statutory body, and in the United Kingdom its composition and duties are prescribed by the Companies Act and the Corporate Governance Code; in the United States, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and NYSE and Nasdaq listing standards require an independent audit committee with specified responsibilities including the oversight of the audit of internal control over financial reporting.

Its distinctive characteristic is a hard independence requirement: the committee must be composed of independent non-executive directors, and in the US it must include at least one financial expert. It typically has between three and five members and reports directly to shareholders in some jurisdictions.

What the audit committee should actually receive is often a matter of confusion. It is not the detailed financial statements and it is not the general risk reporting of the whole enterprise. Its core content is the assurance chain over financial reporting and the effectiveness of the control environment supporting it: the external audit plan and findings, the internal audit plan and findings with a focus on financial and control matters, the internal auditor's annual assessment, management's response to findings, any material control deficiency, the independence and quality of external audit, and the auditor's non-audit services. Reporting line: the committee chairs the meeting without the executive management team present for the private session with the internal and external auditors.

A mature audit committee will also spend time on the audit plan itself, challenging the risk-based selection rather than accepting it. Accepting the plan without challenge is one of the most common ways a board loses its most valuable lever over audit coverage.
bullets: Statutory in most jurisdictions, with prescribed independence requirements
Typically three to five independent non-executive members, often including a financial expert
Core content: external and internal audit results, material control deficiencies, auditor independence, non-audit services
Holds a private session with internal and external auditors without management present
Challenges the audit plan rather than accepting the coverage as presented

sections.heading: The board risk committee (or risk and assurance committee)
sections.body:
The board risk committee oversees the enterprise risk management framework, the risk appetite and the overall risk profile, and it monitors the effectiveness of the risk management and compliance functions. Its purpose is forward-looking and strategic: what could prevent the organisation achieving its objectives, and is the organisation's response proportionate?

It typically includes a mix of independent non-executive directors and one or more executives, and it may also carry responsibility for non-financial risk - operational risk, conduct risk, third-party risk, health and safety, reputational risk - where the organisation has separated these from financial risk. In the United Kingdom, the board risk committee is expected by the Corporate Governance Code to have the primary responsibility for advising the board on risk appetite and the effectiveness of the risk management system and internal control systems.

Its standing content should be: the enterprise risk profile against appetite, with movements explained; top risks and emerging risks with the treatment position; the risk appetite statements and their application; assurance from the second line on the effectiveness of the risk framework; significant risk acceptances made and any that sit outside appetite; third-party and concentration exposure; and forward-looking horizon items such as emerging regulation, geopolitical exposure and climate risk.

The critical discipline for a risk committee is that it does not receive the work of the executive risk committee as a summary of what was decided. It receives the position, the judgement required, and the recommendation. A risk committee that receives only notifications of decisions already taken is an information forum, not a risk committee.

The other distinctive feature is the escalation route. The risk committee's terms of reference must state the circumstances under which a matter goes to the full board, and the mechanism by which the committee can require the executive to act - including the right to require an external assurance review.
bullets: Forward-looking and strategic: risk appetite, framework effectiveness, risk profile, emerging risk
Typically mixes independent non-executive directors with one or more executives
Often holds non-financial risk where financial risk sits with the audit committee
Receives positions and judgements, not notifications of decisions already taken
Terms of reference must define the escalation route to the full board

sections.heading: The management risk committee and the interface between the three
sections.body:
The management risk committee is not a board committee. It is an executive forum, chaired by a senior executive - often the CRO or the COO - that makes decisions about risk within delegated authority and manages the risk profile day to day. Its work is the input to the board risk committee, not a substitute for it.

The three forums form a chain. The management risk committee identifies and decides on risks within its authority. The board risk committee reviews and challenges the resulting profile, sets appetite and requires action. The audit committee independently assures the controls that produce the assurance behind both. The chain breaks in a characteristic way: the board risk committee reviews what the management committee decided, the management committee discovers the board committee's challenge is advisory, and no decision is ever taken anywhere. Detecting this is one of the most valuable things a GRC professional can do.

The interface points to design explicitly. What does the board risk committee require the management committee to have resolved before a matter is escalated? What does the audit committee need from the risk committee to assure itself about control effectiveness? Who owns the risk data model that both committees rely on? And, critically: when the risk committee and the audit committee have overlapping subject matter - most often operational risk, conduct risk and the effectiveness of the risk framework itself - who is the decision owner for the risk committee's onward decisions? The usual answer is that the risk committee owns risk decisions and the audit committee owns assurance decisions, and the audit committee may request that the risk committee consider something, but the risk committee decides.

A specific and common conflict illustrates the point. Internal audit identifies a significant weakness in a business line's risk identification. The risk committee considers the matter and concludes the residual exposure is within appetite. The audit committee, having commissioned the review, has a different view. The correct resolution is not a turf war between committees but a defined mechanism: a single accountable executive owner for the risk response, a documented position, a decision on whether the treatment is adequate, and escalation to the board if the two committees cannot reach a common view - usually through the board chair or the CEO.
table: What are we doing about risk?
Is the risk position acceptable and the response proportionate?
Is the control and assurance system working?
Is the organisation being directed and controlled?
sections.callout: When two committees cannot agree, the answer is not a compromise meeting. It is a named executive owner for the response and an escalation route that both committees have agreed in advance.

sections.heading: Common design failures
sections.body:
Five failures recur, and all five are structural rather than behavioural.

Overlapping mandates. Two committees with materially the same mandate will produce duplicate work, conflicting advice and, eventually, a forum that dominates by sheer volume of paper. The cure is a written allocation of subject matter, tested against real cases rather than topics.

Insufficient independence on the risk committee. A risk committee composed entirely of executives will confirm the executive's assessment, because nobody in the room will challenge it. At least a majority of independent members is a reasonable minimum, and the chair should be independent.

Composition by title rather than by expertise and behaviour. Boards routinely populate committees by seniority. The better question is: who on this committee will be willing to say, in front of the CEO, that the answer is no. Test candidates against that question.

Terms of reference that describe activities rather than decisions. If the terms of reference list what the committee will do rather than what it will decide, they will produce meetings without outcomes. Every committee should have an explicit list of the decisions it makes.

No escalation route from committee to board. Committees need the ability and the obligation to escalate, including the ability to require an external review, and the full board needs to receive committee escalations promptly. Committees that can only advise upward end up with their recommendations diluted.

Two smaller points worth making. In many organisations the chairs of the audit and risk committees meet together periodically without the executive present - a useful and inexpensive mechanism for coordination. And committee membership renewal is itself a governance risk: long-serving members become invested in the committee's own output, and the board should treat term limits and rotation as a discipline rather than an administrative detail.
bullets: Overlapping mandates: allocate subject matter in writing, tested against real cases
Insufficient independence on the risk committee: majority independent members and an independent chair
Composition by title rather than by expertise and willingness to challenge
Terms of reference that list activities rather than decisions
No escalation route from committee to board, including the ability to require external review
Rotate membership deliberately and treat tenure as a governance risk

examples.title: Three committees and one control, three different conclusions
examples.context: A European insurance group operates a board risk committee, an audit committee and a group risk committee at executive level. Each has its own risk taxonomy and its own reporting pack. When the board risk committee asks about operational resilience, the executive group risk committee has already concluded that no significant issue exists, the audit committee has commissioned a review of the underlying controls, and the second line has reported that the resilience framework itself is not fully implemented. Three bodies, three positions, no single source of truth.
examples.outcome: The GRC director establishes a single enterprise risk taxonomy, a single risk data model and a single reporting calendar. The board risk committee becomes the decision forum for enterprise risk; the group risk committee becomes the executive decision forum with a formal upward submission requirement; the audit committee retains independent assurance and is given visibility of the board risk committee's decisions rather than a parallel set of papers. A standing agenda item at the board risk committee - the audit committee chair's observations - replaces the informal lateral conversation. Within two quarters the three committees are working from the same risk data and the divergence disappears.

examples.title: A risk committee with no independent voice
examples.context: A government-owned healthcare provider's board risk committee consists of the CEO, the CFO, the Chief Medical Officer and two non-executives appointed for their sector expertise. It meets quarterly for ninety minutes and reviews a status pack. When the internal auditor attends to report on the effectiveness of the risk framework, the discussion is limited to resourcing for a remediation plan, and the auditor's concern about whether the framework was appropriate for clinical risk is not taken up.
examples.outcome: The independent members identify the structural problem: the chair is the CEO, there is no independent challenge, and the agenda has no decision items. The board approves a revised structure - an independent chair, a majority of independent members, explicit terms of reference listing the decisions the committee makes, a standing agenda built around the enterprise risk profile and appetite, and a requirement that the internal auditor reports to the committee with an executive withdrawal option. The first quarterly meeting under the new terms produces the first genuine challenge in the committee's history: whether clinical safety risk should sit in the enterprise risk register at all, or be managed entirely outside GRC. That question had been avoided for two years.

practicalExercise.title: Design the committee structure and settle a conflict
practicalExercise.brief: Design a committee structure for a specified organisation and resolve a realistic conflict between two committees. The deliverable should be a structure a board would actually approve, with the reasoning for each design choice stated and the conflict resolved through a defined mechanism rather than a discussion.
steps: Profile the organisation: size, legal structure, sector regulatory load, risk profile, and existing board and committee structure.

List the matters the board must oversee, grouped into financial reporting, risk and assurance, and other board matters. Allocate each to a committee or the full board, and record the allocation in a single table.
For each committee, write the decisions it makes, its membership including independence requirements, its chair, its escalation triggers to the full board, and its minimum annual agenda items.

Construct the conflict: pick a plausible matter where the audit committee and the risk committee have different views, and specify the terms of reference that resolve it - a named executive owner, a required position paper, a decision deadline and an escalation route.
Identify the three ways your design could fail in practice, and for each specify the early indicator that would tell you it is happening.
Write a 200-word recommendation to the board chair explaining the structure and the two changes that matter most from their current arrangement.
practicalExercise.deliverable: A committee structure table (forum, mandate, decisions, membership, chair, escalation), a conflict resolution mechanism written into terms of reference, a failure-mode table with early indicators, and a 200-word recommendation.
evaluationCriteria: Every board-oversight matter is allocated to exactly one forum, with the reasoning visible for the two or three hardest allocations
Each committee's terms specify decisions rather than activities, and each has an explicit escalation route to the board
Independence requirements are stated and are proportionate to the committee's purpose
The conflict is resolved by a defined mechanism with an owner and a deadline, not by agreement in principle
Failure modes are plausible and the early indicators are observable rather than generic
The recommendation is written for a chair, is decision-oriented, and identifies what changes rather than describing the whole design
