Sarbanes-Oxley Act 2002, Section 301 - audit committee independence requirements
NYSE Listed Company Manual Section 303A and Nasdaq Rule 5605 - audit committee composition and charter requirements
OECD Principles of Corporate Governance (2023 revision), Section VI on board committees
The Institute of Internal Auditors, Global Internal Audit Standards (effective January 2025), Domain 1: Governance and Domain 4: Internal Audit Results and Communication
European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority, Governance and Operational Risk Function Guidelines

items.title: Executive Accountabilities: CISO, CIO, CRO, DPO
items.summary: Four executive roles sit at the centre of enterprise GRC, and confusing them is a common source of duplicated work and gaps in coverage. This lesson sets out the distinct mandate of the Chief Information Security Officer, the Chief Information Officer, the Chief Risk Officer and the Data Protection Officer, the tensions between them, and what good working arrangements look like.
objectives: Define the primary mandate, typical reporting line and core accountabilities of the CISO, CIO, CRO and DPO
Explain the structural tensions between the four roles and how each is normally resolved
Distinguish the DPO's independence requirements from the general second-line role
Design a working arrangement between the four roles that avoids duplication and coverage gaps

sections.heading: Why the distinctions matter
sections.body:
Every large organisation has these four mandates somewhere, and many have them partly or fully combined. The question is not which model is best - it depends on the sector and the strategy - but what each mandate requires and how conflicts between them are managed.

The distinction that causes the most trouble is between security and IT delivery. The CIO owns the technology estate and the technology strategy. The CISO owns the risk associated with that estate and with information more broadly. When one person holds both roles, the organisation has a delivery owner who is also the assurance owner - the same conflict that would arise if a builder inspected their own foundations. That is sometimes acceptable, and in smaller organisations it is the norm, but the organisation should know it has made that trade and should compensate for it elsewhere, usually through independent second-line reporting to a board committee rather than to the CIO.

The second common confusion is between the Chief Risk Officer and the Chief Information Security Officer. The CRO owns enterprise risk - financial, operational, strategic, compliance and increasingly cyber. The CISO owns information security risk in detail. When cyber risk is reported through the CRO, it can be diluted into an averaged portfolio and lose the technical urgency it needs; when it bypasses the CRO entirely, the enterprise risk picture becomes incomplete. Most mature organisations report cyber risk through the CRO at portfolio level, with the CISO retaining a direct line to the board risk committee.

The third confusion concerns the Data Protection Officer. The DPO is not simply a privacy manager. In the EU, the GDPR requires the DPO to be independent, to report to the highest management level, to have access to resources, and to advise and monitor without taking on decision-making responsibility that would create a conflict. A DPO who owns the processing operations, who designs the product, or who approves the lawful basis, has been placed in a position the regulation specifically prevents.
sections.callout: Combining the CIO and CISO is a legitimate design choice in some organisations. Combining the DPO with the owner of the processing activity is not - the independence requirement is a legal requirement, not a design preference.

sections.heading: The four mandates
sections.body:
The Chief Information Security Officer owns information security: setting the security strategy and policy framework, running the security operations capability, overseeing the security architecture and engineering, managing the security risk register, and leading the response to security incidents. The mandate is both operational - running detection, response, vulnerability management - and advisory to the business on secure design and new business proposals. The CISO is typically a member of the executive committee, reporting to the CEO or to a board committee in some structures, and in regulated sectors often has a statutory or regulatory appointment with reporting obligations to a supervisory authority.

The Chief Information Officer owns the technology strategy, the architecture, the engineering and delivery capability, the IT operating model, the service portfolio, the technology roadmap and, usually, the IT operating budget. The CIO also usually owns the enterprise data and analytics platform, the integration architecture and the technical delivery of new products. Where the CISO also runs security operations, a deliberate split is needed between building the platform and running security on it.

The Chief Risk Officer owns the enterprise risk framework: methodology, appetite, risk identification and assessment, aggregation and reporting, and the second line functions that provide challenge on risk - risk, compliance, and usually business continuity and third-party risk. The CRO's defining characteristic is enterprise-wide breadth and the mandate to aggregate risk across the organisation into a profile the board can govern. The CRO is generally the executive most concerned with the interaction between risks, with scenario analysis, and with whether the risk portfolio is consistent with strategy.

The Data Protection Officer is the independent advisor on data protection law and practice: monitoring compliance, advising on processing activities and new projects, running data protection training, and acting as the contact point for data subjects and supervisory authorities. The mandate is advisory and monitoring. The DPO does not decide how personal data is processed, does not sign off the lawful basis, and does not own the controls - the business does. The DPO advises and monitors; the business decides and is accountable.
table: Information security strategy, security operations, security risk in detail
Technology strategy, architecture, delivery capability, IT services
Enterprise risk framework, appetite, aggregation, second line challenge
Security operations; the decisions of individual business units
Independent advice and monitoring on data protection
Processing decisions, control operation, the lawful basis
Highest management level, independent of the processing owner

sections.heading: Structural tensions and how they are resolved
sections.body:
Four tensions recur in every organisation with these roles, and each has a settled, well-understood resolution. Learning them is worth more than learning any particular framework.

Delivery versus assurance on the technology estate. The CIO needs to ship; the CISO needs to withhold. The resolution is not a veto - a CISO who blocks delivery without offering an alternative becomes the department everyone works around. It is a risk-based gate: security requirements are defined as part of the standards the delivery teams build to, and security effort is triaged by risk. The CISO owns the risk position and the advice; the CIO owns the delivery decision and the accountability for it. Where the two genuinely cannot agree, the matter goes to the executive committee or the CEO with both positions stated.

Portfolio consistency versus specialist urgency. The CRO wants a consistent risk taxonomy and a comparable profile across the enterprise. The CISO wants cyber risk to move fast and be treated with its true severity. The resolution is a defined translation layer: cyber risk is expressed in the enterprise taxonomy and risk appetite so it aggregates correctly, while retaining a direct reporting line to the board risk committee that allows urgency to be preserved. Do not let cyber risk enter the enterprise framework only through an averaging process.

Independence for the DPO. The GDPR requires that the DPO is involved in an advisory and monitoring capacity, reports to the highest management level, has the resources to do the job, and is not instructed on how to perform the tasks. Practically, this means the DPO must have a line that reaches the board - through the audit committee, the risk committee or the CEO - and must be able to escalate without passing through the executive who owns the processing. If the DPO cannot escalate to the board without going through the business owner whose decisions they are monitoring, the arrangement is not compliant in substance regardless of the reporting line on the organisation chart.

Assurance cost versus business momentum. The second line's job is to challenge, and challenge consumes capacity that comes from the business. The resolution is proportionality: the second line sets a risk-based assurance plan, the business funds it as an operating cost of the enterprise, and the second line has the standing to decline engagements outside its plan rather than absorbing them all. An assurance function that absorbs everything is a function that does nothing.
bullets: Delivery versus assurance: risk-based security gates built into delivery standards, not ad hoc vetoes
Portfolio consistency versus specialist urgency: a translation layer into enterprise taxonomy plus a direct line to the board risk committee
DPO independence: escalation to the board must not pass through the owner of the processing decision
Assurance cost versus momentum: a risk-based assurance plan the business funds, with the second line able to decline off-plan work

sections.heading: Building a working arrangement that holds
sections.body:
The four mandates are usually clear enough on paper. What fails is the day-to-day interface, and the failures are predictable.

The most common is duplicate work with no reconciliation. Both the CRO's function and the CISO's function run a risk register; the CISO runs a security issue tracker; the DPO runs a privacy tracker; and the CIO's function runs a technology risk log. Each is locally correct. Together they produce four different answers to the question of how many open high risks the organisation has, and a board that receives all four. The resolution is a single source of truth with a defined ownership split: one enterprise risk register with a defined taxonomy, and status information from the specialist trackers feeding it, rather than parallel registers.

The second is escalation deadlock. A technology risk is owned by the CIO, exceeds appetite, and the CRO's function wants to escalate it to the board risk committee. The CIO's view is that it is a delivery trade-off. The resolution is a written escalation rule that says who escalates, on what basis, with what information, and with what decision the board committee is being asked to make. Escalation deadlock is almost always a design failure rather than a personality failure.

The third is advisory capture. The CISO becomes a delivery function because delivery always has a deadline and security advice rarely does; the DPO becomes a compliance rubber stamp because nobody wants the argument; the CRO becomes a reporting function because producing the board pack is more comfortable than challenging a business unit. The countermeasure in each case is a mandate statement and a reporting line that make challenge the expected behaviour, and a performance assessment that rewards challenge rather than penalising it.

The fourth is meeting overload. Four executives with overlapping remits can generate a disproportionate number of cross-functional meetings. A quarterly executive GRC forum with a single agenda and a written pre-read, replacing several overlapping ones, is usually better than any additional meeting.

Finally, succession. These roles turn over, and each departure removes a large amount of tacit institutional knowledge. The mitigation is boring and effective: written decision rights between the four roles, documented escalation paths, and an institutional memory in the governance artefacts rather than in the individuals. If the arrangement only works because of who currently holds the roles, it is not an operating model.
bullets: One enterprise risk register with a shared taxonomy; specialist trackers feed it rather than duplicating it
Written escalation rules that specify who escalates, on what basis, and the decision sought
Mandates that make challenge the expected behaviour, and performance measures that reward it
Consolidate overlapping meetings into a single forum with a written pre-read
Written decision rights between the four roles, so the arrangement survives changes of personnel
sections.callout: If the four executives disagree about how many high risks the organisation has, the problem is never the executive judgement. It is the data model.

examples.title: One high risk, four registers
examples.context: A global IT services provider runs a cyber risk register in the CISO's function, an enterprise risk register in the CRO's function, a technology risk log in the CIO's function and a privacy risk log in the DPO's function. The board risk committee is shown all four, quarterly. The CIO reports three high technology risks, the CRO reports one, and the CISO reports eleven - mostly the same underlying issues described differently. Directors ask the CRO to reconcile the numbers and he cannot.
examples.outcome: The GRC lead builds one enterprise risk taxonomy with a shared severity model, retains specialist registers as sources, and defines a rule that each enterprise risk has one owner and one entry, with the specialist tracker references attached. Duplicate items are merged with a documented rationale. A standing quarterly reconciliation between the four executives is established with a written pre-read, and the board pack moves to a single enterprise top-risk view with the specialist detail in the annex. Within two quarters the committee is receiving one number set, and the reconciliation meeting is focused on judgement rather than on tidying data.

examples.title: The DPO who could not escalate
examples.context: A healthcare data platform company appoints a DPO who reports to the Chief Product Officer, who owns the processing operations. When the DPO raises a systematic issue - a consent and transparency failure in a new analytics product - the CPO agrees with the substance and asks the DPO not to escalate it while the product is being launched. The launch proceeds. Six months later a supervisory authority asks for the records of the DPO's advice and escalations. The company can show that the DPO raised the issue internally, and cannot show that it went anywhere else.
examples.outcome: The GRC lead reviews the DPO arrangement against the GDPR requirements and identifies three separate failures: the reporting line did not reach the highest management level, the DPO could not escalate without passing through the owner of the decision, and there was no documented procedure for the DPO to inform the board directly. The arrangement is redesigned - the DPO reports to the CEO, attends the risk committee by standing right, has an explicit protocol for escalating to the board, and the internal audit function reviews the operation of that protocol each year. The lesson carried into the GRC standard is that independence is tested by whether escalation is practically possible, not by what the organisation chart says.

practicalExercise.title: Map four mandates onto one organisation and find the gaps
practicalExercise.brief: Define the four executive mandates for an organisation, work out how they interact in practice, and identify where coverage fails. The exercise should produce a working arrangement rather than an organisation chart, and it should surface at least one real conflict with a defined resolution.
steps: Profile the organisation: sector, size, business lines, technology estate, regulatory load and personal data processing.

Write the four mandates in your own words, each with three primary accountabilities and three explicit exclusions. Note where one organisation would combine roles and state the compensating control for each combination you would make.
Identify the artefacts each role would own today - registers, trackers, plans, packs - and list every place the same underlying issue appears in more than one.
Construct the four structural tensions for this organisation and write the specific resolution for each: the decision point, who decides, and what evidence they receive.

Test the DPO independence specifically: trace a specific concern from the DPO to a forum that can act on it, and confirm that the path does not pass through the owner of the processing decision. If it does, redesign it.
Write a one-page executive agreement covering: the four mandates, the shared taxonomy, the escalation rules, the forum structure and the reporting lines to the board.
practicalExercise.deliverable: A one-page executive GRC agreement with the four mandates, the artefact consolidation plan, the escalation rules, the forum structure, and a note on any combination of roles and its compensating control.
evaluationCriteria: Each mandate has three accountabilities and three explicit exclusions, and exclusions are the ones that actually cause disputes
Duplicate artefacts are identified with a specific consolidation approach, not just a call for better integration
Each of the four tensions has a named decision point, a decision owner and the evidence the owner receives
The DPO escalation path is traced end to end and does not route through the processing decision owner
Any combination of roles is accompanied by a compensating control, such as an independent reporting line to a board committee
The agreement is concise enough to be signed and specific enough to settle a real argument

references: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Articles 37 to 39 on the data protection officer
ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Clause 5.3 (Organizational roles, responsibilities and authorities)
ISO/IEC 27005:2022, Clause 5 (Risk management approach) and Clause 7 (Risk management)
The Institute of Internal Auditors, The IIA's Three Lines Model (July 2020)
NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (February 2024), Function 1: GOVERN (GV.RR and GV.RM roles)
Bank of England, Operational resilience: impact tolerances for important business services (framework and guidance, 2021 onward)

items.title: The Three Lines Model in Practice
items.summary: The IIA Three Lines Model is the most widely used statement of how risk responsibility is distributed across an organisation. This lesson explains what the model actually says, the structural rule that makes it work - accountability to the board belongs outside the operating lines - and the practical mechanics of decision rights, escalation and the independence of the third line.
objectives: State the purpose and structure of the IIA Three Lines Model and what each line is accountable for
Explain the model's defining structural rule about board accountability and why independence fails without it
Apply the model to a contested scenario involving an operating manager, a risk function and an internal auditor
Design the decision rights and escalation paths that make the model operate in a specific organisation

sections.heading: What the model says
sections.body:
The IIA's Three Lines Model was published in July 2020 and states that the purpose of governance is to create and sustain an environment of performance and accountability. Its contribution is to show how that environment is supported by three distinct groups of roles, each with a different relationship to the risk.

The governing body - the board or equivalent - is accountable for the organisation's objectives, the governance of risk and the oversight of the framework. Its role is to set direction, set the risk appetite, and hold the executives to account. The model is explicit that the board is not part of any of the three lines: it is the body the lines are accountable to.

The first line owns the risk and manages it. It comprises the people who run the business and are directly responsible for the outcomes: line managers, operations staff, business process owners. The first line is where risk is actually created and where controls are operated. Critically, the first line is not a control function - it is the business doing its job with control built in. Risk ownership cannot be delegated to a second-line function; a second line can advise, challenge and provide assurance, but it cannot own the risk of a business activity it does not run.

The second line supports the first line in managing risk and oversees the risk management and compliance functions. Its purpose is to provide expertise, support and challenge on risk and compliance, and to monitor the risk profile independently of the first line's own view. Risk management, compliance, and typically business continuity, third-party risk, information security and privacy sit here. The second line owns the framework and the methodology, sets the standards, aggregates and analyses the risk position, and provides assurance to the first line that its risk decisions are informed.

The third line provides independent assurance to the board and the governing body on the effectiveness and efficiency of governance, risk management and internal control. It is internal audit. The third line's defining characteristic is independence, and its principal client is the audit committee - not the executive, and not the second line.
table: Running the business and operating controls
Executive, with access to the board
Objective assurance on governance, risk and control
sections.callout: The most common misuse of the model: putting risk ownership in the second line. The second line can tell you how risk should be managed. It cannot accept it on behalf of the business that creates it.

sections.heading: The defining structural rule
sections.body:
One element of the model does more work than any other, and it is the element most often broken. It concerns the accountability of the internal audit function.

The rule: the internal audit function should be accountable to the board or the appropriate governing body, and should report functionally to the board or a board committee - typically the audit committee - while maintaining administrative or operational reporting to the chief executive or the equivalent for resourcing purposes. The model is explicit that this arrangement is essential, because without it the third line cannot be independent.

The reason is structural. Internal audit reports findings that management do not want to hear. If the third line's appointment, budget, performance assessment and daily reporting line all run through the executives whose work it is auditing, its independence is contingent on their goodwill. Goodwill is not a control. In practice the arrangement works because the audit committee approves the internal audit plan, approves the appointment of the chief audit executive, reviews the budget, and meets with the chief audit executive without management present.

This rule has a corollary that organisations find uncomfortable: the executive management team cannot direct the internal audit function's work. Management may set priorities through the audit committee, may respond to findings, and may request additional work - but the plan, the scope of individual engagements and the reporting line are the audit committee's. Where an executive can send internal auditors to investigate a matter and receives a report directly, the third line has been absorbed into the first line.

There is also a distinction worth being precise about, because it is regularly confused: independence of the third line and independence of the second line are different things, and the model treats them differently. The second line is not independent of the first line in the way internal audit is - it is part of the management structure and reports to the executive. But it must be sufficiently separated to perform its challenging role: it must have a reporting line that protects it from the units it challenges, access to the board or a board committee, and the mandate to escalate. The commonly stated principle is that the second line should report to a leader with no responsibility for the operating area being challenged. Where a risk or compliance function reports to the very executive who owns the risk, the challenging function is structurally unable to do its job, no matter how senior its people are.

The model also makes clear that the lines are not three parallel hierarchies of equal status. They have different purposes and different degrees of independence, and the second line's position is the most delicate: it must be close enough to the first line to be useful and far enough away to be credible.
bullets: Internal audit is accountable to the board or appropriate governing body, functionally reporting to the audit committee
Administrative reporting to the CEO may exist for resourcing, but must not create direction of audit work
Management cannot direct the internal audit plan, engagement scope or reporting lines
Second-line independence is distinct: close enough to be useful, far enough to be credible, with a reporting line that protects the challenging role
If the executive being challenged also decides the second line's priorities, the second line cannot function

sections.heading: Decision rights in practice
sections.body:
The model says nothing about who decides what, which is where it is usually translated into practice, and where most disputes originate. A workable translation defines three things for each significant decision: who decides, who must be consulted, and who must be informed.

Start with the obvious rule and note where it is wrong. The first line decides operational matters within risk appetite. The second line advises and challenges but does not take the decision. The third line does not decide anything about the business, ever - it decides the scope of its own work, subject to the audit committee. Where this rule is applied rigidly, it breaks in one direction: business managers will wait for the second line to clear a decision before taking it, which converts advice into a veto and slows the organisation to a standstill while building a queue.

The correction is that the decision stays with the first line, but the first line must take the second line's position on the record. Where the first line decides against the second line's advice, that is permitted - it is the business's risk to own - but the record must show that the advice was given, what the reasoning was, and who in the executive accepted the residual exposure. This mechanism is what converts the model from a description into a working arrangement. Without it, the second line either becomes a veto, which destroys the model, or becomes advisory only, which destroys the challenge.

The escalation rules then follow the appetite. Where a decision sits inside appetite and the first line and second line agree, it is made and recorded. Where it sits inside appetite but they disagree, it goes to the accountable executive who owns the exposure, with both positions documented. Where it sits outside appetite, it escalates to whoever set the appetite, typically the board risk committee, and the decision to accept outside appetite is recorded with an explicit board-level acceptance. Where a legal obligation is breached by the decision, no risk acceptance is available at all - the point was made in the compliance module and it holds here.

The third line fits into the model through the audit committee rather than through these decision paths. Internal audit tests whether the arrangement is working; it does not participate in it.
table: Inside appetite, first and second line agree
Accountable executive decides, owning the residual exposure
Both positions, the reasoning and the named acceptor
Escalates to the level that set the appetite
Explicit acceptance at that level, with time limit and monitoring
Would breach a legal or contractual obligation
Not a risk decision - fix or stop the activity
Compliance assessment retained with the decision
sections.callout: The second line advises and challenges. The first line owns the decision. The record is what keeps both of those true at once.

sections.heading: Where the model breaks down
sections.body:
Five failure patterns account for most of the dissatisfaction practitioners report with the model, and each has a recognisable early indicator.

The second line becomes the business's risk owner in practice. Indicator: business units escalate decisions to the second line and wait, and the second line's queue grows. Cause: the executive does not own the residual exposure and wants the comfort of a second-line sign-off, so it lets the second line take the decision by default.

The third line is captured. Indicator: the internal audit plan is materially shaped by executive preference, and internal auditors report to executives rather than to the audit committee. Cause: administrative reporting line treated as the real one.

The lines are used as an organisational chart rather than a behaviour model. Indicator: the exercise of labelling a team as first, second or third line produced no change to any decision or escalation path. This is the most common outcome when the model is deployed as a reclassification exercise, which is why it must be deployed as a decision-rights exercise.

The first line is materially absent. Indicator: control operation is described as a second line or central function activity, and business staff describe their role in risk management as limited to following the policy. Cause: control design that removes all judgement from the business, or a risk function that has taken over the first line's work.

Escalation is theoretical. Indicator: the escalation protocol has never been used, or was used once and the outcome was not recorded. Cause: escalation paths defined without defined decision rights, thresholds or time limits at the top. A protocol that has never been tested is a policy, not a capability.

Two further practical points. The model is not a permanent structure - the distribution of work shifts as the organisation changes, and a rigid allocation becomes an obstacle. And in organisations with a strong external assurance dependency - a heavily regulated financial institution, for instance - the internal audit function is itself subject to independent review, and the model should accommodate that external layer rather than pretend the third line is the only assurance.
bullets: Second line owning decisions in practice: queue growth and executive discomfort with residual exposure
Third line captured: audit plan shaped by executive preference and reporting lines that bypass the audit committee
The model deployed as reclassification with no change to decision rights - the most common failure
First line materially absent: controls operated centrally, business staff with no defined risk role
Escalation never tested: protocols that exist but have no thresholds, owners or recorded outcomes
sections.callout: A protocol that has never been exercised is a policy. Capability is demonstrated by an escalation that happened, was decided, and was recorded.

examples.title: An internal audit function reporting to the CFO
examples.context: A mid-sized industrial group's internal audit function reports to the CFO, who also owns the finance systems that internal audit has repeatedly found to have access segregation weaknesses. The audit committee receives reports, but the function has never been able to complete the annual plan on schedule; the last three audits of finance systems were deferred after executive requests. The new CISO notes that the deferred audits are not recorded anywhere.
examples.outcome: The GRC lead identifies the structural failure the Three Lines Model is designed to prevent: administrative and functional reporting have collapsed into one, and the executive most affected by the findings controls the audit plan. The remediation is not about individuals - it is about the arrangement: the internal audit function is made functionally accountable to the audit committee, which approves the annual plan, the appointment of the chief audit executive and the resourcing, with a standing private session without management present. Deferred audits are logged as plan changes reported to the committee rather than as silent omissions. Within a year the finance systems audits are complete and the findings are being closed, and the chief audit executive reports the plan to the committee directly.

examples.title: The second-line veto in a telecom operator
examples.context: A telecom operator's enterprise risk function reviews every material business case before approval, with a two-week standard turnaround. Marketing campaigns increasingly wait for a risk sign-off, and the risk function's queue grows. The CRO insists the reviews are necessary for control, but the commercial director general observes that the organisation is losing campaign windows and that the risk function has effectively become an approval stage nobody designed.
examples.outcome: The GRC lead applies the model's decision-rights test: the first line owns the decision, the second line advises, and the record preserves both positions. Campaign risk reviews are reclassified from approval to advice, with a defined service level of five working days and a template of the advice the business needs. Where the business proceeds against the advice, the reasoning and the accepting executive are recorded, and a threshold - campaigns above a defined spend or with defined characteristics - is escalated to the executive committee. The queue collapses because approvals were the expensive part. The CRO keeps the challenge, but challenge now happens as advice plus a recorded exception rather than as a gate.

practicalExercise.title: Translate the Three Lines Model into decision rights
practicalExercise.brief: Take a contested decision in an organisation and use the Three Lines Model to work out who decides, who advises, who is informed, and what gets recorded. The exercise must end with a concrete decision path, not a diagram.
steps: Describe the organisation and identify three functions and the individuals who hold the contested decisions - typically a business unit head, a risk or compliance manager, and an internal audit manager.
For each of the five decisions, write a one-line decision statement and identify the primary risk it creates.
Classify each function as first, second or third line and justify it in terms of who owns the outcome, not who performs the activity.

Apply the decision-rights test to each decision: inside appetite with agreement, inside appetite with disagreement, outside appetite, and would-breach-obligation. Write the decision-maker, the required record and the escalation threshold for each case.
Draft the escalation protocol for one case, including the trigger, the information pack, the decision rights at each level, the time limits and the record of the outcome.
Identify one structural change you would make to the organisation to prevent the model breaking down as described in the lesson, and specify the early indicator that would tell you it is working.

items.title: Internal Audit vs External Audit
items.summary: Internal audit and external audit differ in mandate, independence, reporting and consequence, and confusing the two leads to bad design and worse advice. This lesson compares them properly, covers the specific external audit types a GRC professional will encounter, and explains how to manage the relationships between internal audit, external audit and the regulator without either party being captured by the other.
objectives: Compare internal and external audit across mandate, independence, reporting, resourcing and the consequences of findings
Distinguish the main types of external audit - financial, regulatory, certification, supplier and due diligence - and what each is actually testing
Explain the role internal audit plays in relation to external audit, including coordination and the avoidance of duplication
Manage a situation where external audit findings, internal audit findings and management self-assessment conflict

sections.heading: The real difference is the source of the mandate
sections.body:
Both internal and external auditors test controls and both report findings. The distinction that explains everything else is where the mandate comes from and who the work is for.

Internal audit is a function of the organisation, mandated by the board or the audit committee, whose primary client is the board. Its purpose is to add value by providing objective and independent assurance and advice on whether the organisation's governance, risk management and internal control processes are working. Its findings are internal management information first, and the board decides what becomes public. It is resourced from the organisation's budget and its performance is assessed by the audit committee.

External audit is engaged by someone with the authority to require it - the board, shareholders, a regulator, a customer, a lender, a certification body. Its mandate comes from outside the organisation, and its report is addressed to that party. The critical consequence is that external auditors report what the engagement requires them to report, including matters management considers confidential, because their duty runs to the engaging party. External audit findings are also, in most regimes, a matter of public record or at least of record to the regulator.

Independence follows from the mandate, and both sides of the table have a legitimate claim to it - from different directions. Internal audit needs independence from management, so that it can report unwelcome findings, which is why it reports functionally to the audit committee. External audit needs independence from the audited entity, so that its opinion is worth paying for, which is why fees, non-audit services and long tenure are constrained by regulator rules.

The two forms also differ in consequence. A failed external audit opinion is a market event, with financing, covenant and regulatory consequences and personal consequences for signatories in some cases. A failed internal audit finding is an internal management matter that becomes a public event only if management fails to act on it. This asymmetry is why internal audit findings are frequently higher in volume and lower in stakes, and why the risk to the organisation is usually not the finding but the failure to close it.

An external party with authority to require it
The engaging party - shareholders, regulator, customer, certification body
Assurance and advice on governance, risk and control effectiveness
A specific opinion, assurance conclusion or certification decision
From management, via functional reporting to the audit committee
From the entity, via ethical codes and regulatory independence rules
All governance, risk and control activity across the entity
Defined by the engagement and its terms

Adverse opinion, qualification, loss of certification, regulatory and market consequences

sections.heading: The external audits you will actually meet
sections.body:
External audit is not one thing, and the differences matter for how you prepare, who you talk to and what you can share.

Financial statement audit is the statutory external audit of the financial statements, conducted to obtain reasonable assurance and to express an opinion on whether the statements give a true and fair view. Its scope is driven by materiality and by the audit risk model, and it is not primarily a control audit - although the understanding of controls needed to design substantive procedures is substantial. In the UK, the auditor also reports on the directors' report and, for listed companies, on the consistency of the strategic report and the governance information with the financial statements.

Regulatory audit is performed by a supervisor or by an audit firm appointed by the supervisor, usually on a risk-based cycle across a regulated population. It tests compliance with the regulatory regime, and it frequently forms the evidence base for supervisory action. Where you are in a regulated industry, the relationship between the regulatory audit, your internal audit and your supervisory relationship is the single most consequential set of relationships in your GRC function.

Certification audit is conducted by an accredited certification body against a management system standard - ISO/IEC 27001, ISO 37301, ISO 9001, ISO 22301. It is not an audit of your controls in isolation but of your management system's effectiveness in achieving the standard's stated results. Certification audits are typically conducted in two stages: a documentation review stage, then an on-site implementation stage, with periodic surveillance between certification audits.

Supplier and third-party audits are performed by your organisation, or by an agent on your behalf, on a supplier. These are external in the sense that the auditor is not part of the supplier, but the mandate and the client are yours. The distinctive feature is that you are simultaneously the client and the party relying on the conclusion, which creates a conflict that must be managed through the contract and the acceptance criteria.

Transaction and due diligence audits sit in the same category: financial or operational diligence before an acquisition, an investment or a disposal, often conducted under tight confidentiality constraints that limit what you can tell the other side.

The distinction to carry forward is that external audit asks a specific question under a specific mandate, and its conclusions are addressed to someone other than the operating business. Good GRC practice is to treat each external audit as a separate engagement with its own scope, criteria and reporting line - not as an extension of the internal audit plan.
bullets: Financial statement audit: opinion on true and fair view, materiality-driven scope, not primarily a control audit
Regulatory audit: supervisor-led, risk-based across a regulated population, feeds supervisory action
Certification audit: two stages, documentation review then implementation, with surveillance between
Supplier and third-party audit: you are both client and relying party; manage the conflict through the contract
Transaction and due diligence audit: tight confidentiality, limits on disclosure to the other side of a deal

sections.heading: The relationship between internal and external audit
sections.body:
The two functions are complements, and a mature organisation manages the relationship actively rather than leaving it to chance.

Internal audit's principal contribution to the external audit relationship is threefold. First, coverage: internal audit's work across the year provides the external auditor with an understanding of control operation that reduces the extent of substantive testing needed - this is genuinely valuable and quantifiable, and it is one of the clearest arguments for funding internal audit. Second, challenge: internal audit's findings are an independent check on the reliability of management's control representations. Third, forward focus: internal audit can identify control weaknesses in areas the external audit has not yet reached, allowing remediation before the external audit finds it.

External audit's contributions to internal audit are equally real. The external auditor's independent assessment of significant areas is a reliable input to the internal audit risk assessment. The external audit's knowledge of the organisation and its understanding of control weaknesses can be shared, subject to professional independence restrictions. And the external audit's report is a source of assurance that internal audit can rely on for some areas, which directly affects how internal audit allocates its own coverage.

What must be avoided is duplication dressed up as coordination. Internal and external audit plans should be reviewed together - typically as part of the audit committee's cycle - so that coverage gaps are closed and the same area is not examined twice in the same year without a reason. But the plans are not merged. The external auditor sets their own scope and must remain independent of the internal audit function; the internal auditor sets their own plan based on internal risk assessment, not external audit coverage. Internal audit should never be tasked with performing work that supports the external auditor's opinion, because doing so compromises the independence of both.

The second thing to avoid is the reverse dependency: management using the external audit as a substitute for internal audit. Where the annual internal audit plan is reduced because external audit covers some area, the organisation loses continuous coverage between annual external audits, and it loses the risk-based view that internal audit is uniquely positioned to provide. External audit does not reduce the need for internal audit; it changes what internal audit should concentrate on.

A third management point is information flow with regulators. Internal audit findings that would be relevant to a supervisor should reach the supervisor through the established regulatory channel - usually the compliance function or the board - rather than directly. Internal auditors are not the right channel for regulatory disclosure, and doing it informally creates both a regulatory problem and an internal one.
bullets: Internal audit contributes coverage knowledge, independent challenge on management representations, and early warning of control weaknesses
External audit contributes an independent assessment, risk insight and assurance that internal audit can rely on for coverage planning
Review both plans together at committee level, but do not merge them and do not task internal audit with supporting the external opinion
External audit does not reduce the need for internal audit; it changes internal audit's concentration areas
Regulatory disclosure flows through the established compliance or board channel, not through internal audit

sections.heading: When the three versions of the truth disagree
sections.body:
A recurring and uncomfortable scenario: management self-assessment says a control is effective; internal audit says it is not; external audit says something in between, or says something different entirely. Each party has a legitimate reason for its view, and the disagreement is not resolved by seniority.

Start by understanding why they differ. External audit applies materiality and tests controls with a sample, often on a different population and at a different time from internal audit. Internal audit may use a different criterion - often the organisation's own standard rather than the standard the external auditor applies. Management self-assessment is typically the least reliable because it is unaccompanied by evidence and is subject to optimism. The reconciliation exercise is to establish, for each control in dispute, the criterion being applied, the population, the sample and the period. In a high proportion of genuine disputes, the disagreement is not about the facts but about the criterion, and once the criterion is agreed the findings reconcile.

Second, establish the hierarchy of evidence, which is not simply that external audit wins. External auditors are not infallible and their scope is constrained by materiality and by the nature of a reasonable assurance engagement. Internal auditors may look deeper on the control in question and may reach a more accurate conclusion. The rule that works: an organisation's position on a control should be the best-supported position, whatever the source, and a disagreement between internal and external audit is a trigger for investigation, not a reason to prefer one firm's conclusion.

Third, recognise the cases where the disagreement is not reconcilable and must be escalated. If the external auditor concludes a control is ineffective and management disagrees, the matter is a disagreement with the auditor that, in most regimes, must be resolved through the audit committee and may require disclosure. If internal audit finds a material weakness that management has not accepted, the escalation path and the disclosure implications of internal control over financial reporting apply. These are governance events, not technical disagreements.

Finally, be careful about the human dynamics. Management teams often treat an adverse external finding as an attack and an adverse internal finding as a coaching opportunity. The correct response to both is the same: identify the criterion, obtain the evidence, establish the facts, and then act. The one behaviour to avoid is negotiating the conclusion rather than testing the assertion.
bullets: Reconcile by establishing criterion, population, sample and period - many disputes are criterion disputes
Management self-assessment without evidence is the least reliable of the three views
Do not adopt a hierarchy of sources; use the best-supported position and investigate disagreements
Adverse findings and material weaknesses follow the escalation and disclosure paths, not the negotiating table
sections.callout: When an audit conclusion is challenged, test the assertion, not the conclusion. Most disagreements are about criteria, not facts.

examples.title: A regulator's audit and an internal audit plan in a bank
examples.context: A commercial bank's supervisory examination covers credit risk, conduct and operational resilience. Separately, internal audit has planned a review of the same operational resilience framework for the same period. Management proposes to cancel the internal audit review, arguing the regulator is already covering it and the regulator's findings carry more weight with the board.
examples.outcome: The chief audit executive explains why that reasoning fails on both counts. The regulator's examination is risk-based across the regulated population and will not deliver the depth of a focused internal review; internal audit can be more thorough on a single framework. More importantly, internal audit's independence from management means its findings carry a different and often more credible weight internally. The decision is instead to sequence the work - internal audit's review is retimed to complete before the regulator arrives, its findings inform the bank's response to the supervisor, and the two audits share the evidence base without duplicating testing. The board is briefed on the distinction between covering an area and covering it adequately, and the internal audit plan is not reduced.

examples.title: Certification audit, internal audit and a management self-assessment
examples.context: An IT services company is in year one of ISO/IEC 27001 certification. The certification body asks for evidence that the internal audit programme has been performed across the ISMS scope. Management produces a spreadsheet of control self-assessments marked complete, the internal audit plan covering only two of the eleven processes, and a management review pack asserting that the ISMS is effective. The certification body's Stage 2 auditor identifies the discrepancy.
examples.outcome: The gap is not the spreadsheet - it is that the organisation has treated management self-assessment as internal audit. The corrective path is to resource and perform an actual internal audit programme covering the full scope within the required cycle, with independence from the process owners, evidenced by workpapers, and reporting into the management review with findings and corrective actions. The self-assessment spreadsheet is retained but relabelled for what it is - an operational control monitoring record that supports, but does not replace, the internal audit conclusion. The certification body accepts this and issues a certification with an observation. The broader lesson for the GRC lead is that an internal audit programme is the backbone of an ISMS and should be built as part of the system, not retrofitted at audit time.

practicalExercise.title: Build a coordinated external and internal audit plan
practicalExercise.brief: For a specified organisation, identify the external audits it faces over a year, design a coordinated plan with internal audit, and rehearse the handling of a disagreement between the three sources of assurance. The deliverable is a plan that an audit committee could approve.
steps: Profile the organisation and list every external audit it will face in the next twelve months: financial, regulatory, certification, customer-driven and supplier-side, with the body conducting it, the scope, the expected date and the reporting line.
